articles.title: Microsoft earnings preview: Employee buyouts, AI spending and a new financial scorecard
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Microsoft’s earnings report Wednesday will come two days after the company offered buyouts to about 60,000 people , roughly a quarter of its employees. The call gives executives their first chance to say what the offer will cost, and to explain how it fits with the company’s long-term view of its workforce.

Whether or not they go into those details, it’s one of several issues to watch in Wednesday’s report, the first under Microsoft’s new reporting structure. Anthropic’s IPO filing on Monday adds another storyline, showing how much the Claude maker has agreed to spend on Microsoft’s cloud.

Coming into the report, Microsoft’s stock is near its high. Microsoft closed Monday at $532.60, about 2% below its record close of $543.45 on Oct. 13, after gaining roughly $1.4 trillion in market value since late June.
Here are the key numbers and issues heading into Microsoft’s results for the first quarter of its 2027 fiscal year, ended Sept. 30.

Core numbers: Analysts expect revenue of $90.75 billion, up nearly 17% from a year ago, and earnings of $4.72 per share, up 14%, according to Yahoo Finance . Microsoft’s own forecast was $89.85 billion to $90.95 billion, so Wall Street is looking for a result near the top of that range.
In July, Microsoft reported $90 billion in revenue for the June quarter, well above the $87.7 billion analysts expected.
A new scorecard: Microsoft announced in September that it would sort its business into two groups instead of the three it had used since 2015. This is the first quarter under the new setup.

The first, dubbed Agents and Infra, includes Azure, Microsoft 365, Dynamics, LinkedIn’s recruiting and sales tools, and server and productivity licensing. It brought in 81% of Microsoft’s revenue and 88% of its operating income in fiscal 2026, based on figures Microsoft recast under the new structure.
Microsoft expects Agents and Infra revenue of $75.15 billion to $75.75 billion this quarter, which would be growth of about 22% to 23%, by GeekWire’s calculation.
The other group, Devices and Consumer, includes Windows, Xbox and search advertising. Microsoft expects it to bring in $14.7 billion to $15.2 billion, down 5% to 8% from a year earlier.

Azure, in dollars: Microsoft started disclosing Azure’s annual revenue last year, when it passed $75 billion, and topped $100 billion in fiscal 2026. Starting this quarter, it reports the figure every quarter. It also changed what counts as Azure: GitHub’s cloud business and Security Copilot now fall under Microsoft 365, and its healthcare cloud moved to a new industry unit.

Counted that way, Azure brought in $29.4 billion in the June quarter, up 42%. Microsoft expects growth of 44% to 45% this quarter, not counting currency fluctuations, which would put Azure at roughly $32 billion, by GeekWire’s calculation. That compares with the roughly 45% Microsoft projected in July, under the old definition.

Hitting that forecast may not be enough. Investors are looking for about 46%, BNP Paribas analyst Stefan Slowinski wrote in a note Monday. In January, Azure beat Microsoft’s own forecast and the stock still fell 10% , because investors had privately expected more.
“Azure moves the stock, but the read that matters is whether capacity is absorbed as fast as it lands,” wrote Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives in a note last week.

Capital spending: Microsoft expects capital expenditures of more than $50 billion for the quarter, which would be a record. That’s up from $41 billion in the June quarter and $34.9 billion a year earlier.

An accounting change reduces what Microsoft reports as capital spending, without reducing its planned investment. Microsoft now assumes its data center buildings will last 25 years instead of 15. As a result, more of its data center leases will be classified in a way that doesn’t count as capital spending, CFO Amy Hood said on the July earnings call.

That change alone lowered Microsoft’s capital spending estimate for calendar 2026 to about $175 billion, from the roughly $190 billion it projected in April. Hood said the company’s actual spending plans hadn’t changed.

Cloud margins: Microsoft Cloud gross margin came in at 65% last quarter, better than expected but down from a year earlier. Microsoft said it expects the figure to be relatively stable this quarter. It also expects operating margins to be roughly flat with a year ago.

Workforce: The new “voluntary exit” offer, announced Monday by Chief People Officer Amy Coleman, covers participating teams in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. It has no age or tenure requirement and extends to some vice presidents. Employees have until the first week of December to decide, and Microsoft hasn’t said how much the offer will cost or when it will record the charge.

For the spring retirement program, Hood disclosed the cost on the April earnings call: about $900 million, with roughly $350 million in cost of revenue and $550 million in operating expenses. The charge showed up in the following quarter. About 30% of the 8,750 eligible employees accepted.

The new offer is less generous. It matches Microsoft’s standard severance, without the extended healthcare of the spring program, and the company expects a much smaller share of people to take it. But the pool of eligible employees is nearly seven times larger.

Microsoft says the offer doesn’t mean it needs fewer people. Coleman said in July that the company was studying whether to make voluntary exits a regular part of managing its workforce. It has told investors to expect operating margins roughly flat this quarter and down less than a point for the full fiscal year, even with record capital spending.

Nadella has addressed this before. In a July 2025 memo to employees , after Microsoft laid off about 15,000 people, he acknowledged the “uncertainty and seeming incongruence” of thriving financially while cutting jobs. “This is the enigma of success in an industry that has no franchise value,” he wrote .

In his annual shareholder letter last week, he focused on Microsoft’s spending on AI infrastructure. “Based on the demand we see and the efficiencies we are driving, I am confident in the long-term returns on our investments,” Nadella wrote. “We are building against a growing book of business tied to this secular shift.”

Microsoft had about 223,000 employees as of June 30 , before it cut 4,800 jobs in July and more in September . The Information reported this month that Azure President Girish Bablani told leaders in his group to find ways to cut costs by at least 20%. Microsoft called the report inaccurate and said Azure leadership had not directed teams to develop cost-cutting plans.

Copilot: Microsoft said in July that businesses were paying for more than 30 million Microsoft 365 Copilot seats, up from 20 million in April. That’s still only about 7% of the more than 450 million commercial Microsoft 365 seats.

The bigger change is in how Microsoft charges for Copilot and its other AI tools. In July it added usage-based billing alongside per-seat pricing. It’s also pushing customers toward E7, a new premium bundle that includes Copilot. Microsoft expects Microsoft 365 commercial cloud revenue to grow about 17% this quarter, not counting currency swings, a number that now includes GitHub.

The BNP Paribas analyst Slowinski, who attended Microsoft’s Frontier Tour event in London last week, wrote that partners are seeing more customers roll out Copilot company-wide. Partners also told him that Microsoft now ties 35% of E7 sales incentives to how much customers use features like Cowork.

Anthropic and OpenAI: Anthropic’s S-1 filing shows the company has committed to spend at least $44.9 billion with Microsoft from November 2026 to May 2033, up from the $30 billion Azure commitment announced last November. That’s well below its minimum commitments to Amazon ($110 billion) and Google ($114.5 billion).
Microsoft agreed last year to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic. Its results for the June quarter included a $3.2 billion gain on that investment.

OpenAI remains the bigger factor. Microsoft’s commercial remaining performance obligation (RPO), the measure of signed contracts it hasn’t yet delivered on, reached $678 billion last quarter, up 84% from a year earlier. Without OpenAI, the backlog grew 25%. OpenAI told investors its annualized revenue approached $50 billion at the end of September, The Information reported , lower than earlier reports of about $70 billion.

Windows: Microsoft expects revenue from Windows licenses sold to PC makers, along with its own devices, to fall a little more than 20%. Higher memory prices are making PCs more expensive, and PC makers are still working through extra inventory.
What’s next: Alphabet also reports Wednesday afternoon, and Amazon reports Thursday, setting up a side-by-side look at Azure, Google Cloud and AWS.
Anthropic is aiming to go public the week of Nov. 16, according to the Wall Street Journal .
Check back Wednesday afternoon for coverage.

articles.title: Seattle’s Kivo Health raises $10M to bring lung disease rehab into patients’ homes
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Seattle-based Kivo Health today announced $10 million in funding to help increase access to its services, which target older adults with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The Series A round brings the startup’s total funding to more than $16 million.

Kivo ships equipment to patients’ homes and provides a nine-week program of therapist-led, live video sessions focused on exercise, breathing techniques and disease management. The company provides ongoing support following the program and says it uses AI to handle administrative tasks and communicate with patients, supporting its clinicians.

“We’re using the funding to build our AI health coach to blend AI-led care with human-led care,” Dr. Victor Sadauskas , Kivo’s co-founder and CEO, said via email. That pairing, he added, will help patients manage their chronic disease over the long term.
The company has approximately 50 employees, including clinicians.

COPD is an incurable lung disease in which damaged airways and air sacs make breathing difficult and can worsen over time. Common symptoms include shortness of breath, a persistent cough and fatigue. COPD is the third leading cause of death globally and the fifth in the U.S.

However, there are effective treatments to improve the condition, though many patients are not able to easily access care. A study of Medicare beneficiaries with COPD found that only 3.7% received pulmonary rehabilitation in 2012.

Kivo reports that a peer-reviewed study of its program found improvements in participants’ symptoms, physical function and mental health. The company also funded an analysis that estimated its model could reduce annual health care spending by $8,245 per member through fewer hospitalizations, ER visits and time in nursing homes.
Kivo says its program is covered by Medicare, Medicaid and private insurers including UnitedHealthcare, Humana, Blue Cross, Aetna and Priority Health.

“By thoughtfully combining high quality clinical care with AI, we can now scale proactive, accessible care to every senior, improving symptoms and reducing avoidable costs,” Sadauskas said in a statement.

Sadauskas launched Kivo in 2023 with co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Vaughn Koch . Sadauskas previously was an emergency medicine physician for Kaiser Permanente and a senior investment fellow with Life Science Angels. Koch is a serial entrepreneur who sold his startup Movity to Trulia in 2010.
While its current focus is COPD, Kivo aims to expand into other costly chronic conditions affecting older adults.
Allumia Ventures led the round, with participation from Corewell Health Ventures, Y Combinator, Heuristic Capital and MassMutual Ventures.

articles.title: Seattle startup Avante raises $30M to bring AI agents to corporate benefits teams
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Avante , the maker of an AI platform to help companies manage employee health care and other benefits, has landed a $30 million Series A round.

Frist Cressey Ventures led the round, with participation from Sorenson Capital, Hearst Ventures, Morgan Stanley Next Level Fund and existing investor Fuse. The new funding, announced Tuesday , brings Seattle-based Avante’s total raised to $40 million, following a $10 million seed round led by Fuse in 2024.

Benefits are one of employers’ biggest costs. Avante’s AI agents do work like comparing vendor contracts against actual claims, reviewing plan documents for errors and preparing for renewals. Employees can also use the platform to ask questions about their own coverage.
The startup plans to use the cash to expand internationally and develop more AI agents, building on a beta release of its “Ava Agents” last week.

Avante says it now has more than 70 customers, including Samsung Semiconductor, Real Chemistry, Zscaler and News Corp, and that bookings grew nearly fivefold over the past year. The platform reaches more than 385,000 employees and family members, according to the company.

Avante was founded in 2023 by CEO Rohan D’Souza ; Carly Eckert , a physician and epidemiologist who serves as head of innovation and impact; and executive chairman Kabir Shahani , the co-CEO of Amperity.

D’Souza and Eckert previously worked as executives at health care automation company Olive AI, which shut down in 2023. The startup emerged from stealth in early 2024 and launched publicly in April 2025.

“Benefits teams are responsible for one of the largest and most consequential investments their companies make, yet they’re still operating with outdated information, archaic spreadsheets, and technology built for another era,” D’Souza said in a statement.
Avante is pitching its software as employers face rising health care costs. Large employers are projecting a median 9.2% increase for 2027, the company said.

The startup competes with benefits and HR software providers such as Workday, ADP, Deel and Rippling. It has also signed partnerships with benefits advisory firms including Gallagher, OneDigital, Segal Benz, Howden and USI Insurance Services.
Avante ranks No. 156 on the GeekWire 200 , our list of top Pacific Northwest tech startups.

articles.title: Nuclear power at sea: Seattle startup targets Norway for ships and floating power plants
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Emerald Nuclear today announced a $2.1 million award from The Research Council of Norway to support its efforts to bring nuclear energy to the shipping industry and offshore power. The Seattle-based startup is developing high-temperature gas reactors that use an encapsulated fuel designed to resist meltdowns.

“This award will enable Emerald Nuclear to work directly with our marine partners to validate integration of our technology with their state-of-the-art marine power distribution and control systems,” said Wesley Deason , co-founder and CEO.
The funding supports Norway’s Marine Nuclear Propulsion System Pilot project, which is being led by Emerald Nuclear’s Norwegian subsidiary.

Shipping accounts for roughly 3% of global carbon dioxide emissions, making it a significant target for lower-carbon energy solutions. Some ferries serving shorter routes are adopting hybrid-electric propulsion. Shipping companies are exploring methanol, ammonia, biofuels and other alternatives to heavy fuel oil, but their climate benefits depend on how those fuels are produced and used.
Nuclear reactors have powered U.S. Navy submarines for more than 70 years. Now, a new wave of companies is working to expand nuclear power’s role in commercial shipping and other marine applications.

The award supports an early development step for Emerald Nuclear, with substantial work remaining before commercial deployment. The company has yet to build its first reactor, and its plans will require additional financing, regulatory approvals and a reliable fuel supply. The startup has previously received an undisclosed amount of funding from angel investors.

Emerald Nuclear has five employees , most of them in Norway, and is targeting two applications: offshore ships that help construct facilities like oil platforms and wind turbines and lay deep-sea cables, and floating power plants for remote communities. Each reactor is designed to produce 5 megawatts (6,705 horsepower), according to the company.

Bringing nuclear to the marine environment poses several significant challenges. They include safety issues, regulations for vessels traveling internationally, management of nuclear fuel and waste, and the way shipping companies frequently buy and sell vessels.
Deason said the company’s approach helps address those concerns:
Emerald Nuclear is designing its technology “to integrate with the unique power needs of the ship, but also to meet the ways that the maritime industry does business,” Deason said.

Other companies pursuing nuclear ship propulsion include Core Power, newcleo and Blykalla. Core Power, Westinghouse, Saltfoss Energy and Prodigy Clean Energy are also developing floating nuclear power stations. Russia’s state-owned Rosatom already has nuclear-powered icebreakers and a floating nuclear power plant in operation.
Prior to launching Emerald Nuclear , Deason, a nuclear engineer, worked for Ultra Safe Nuclear Corp. (USNC) developing reactors for space-based applications.

During his tenure at the Seattle company, a professor from the Norwegian University of Science and Technology approached USNC about applications for the maritime sector. USNC declared bankruptcy in October 2024 and the deal wasn’t pursued. But the idea interested Deason and Hallgeir Juliebø , a Norwegian entrepreneur who had been a consultant with USNC. The two co-founded Emerald Nuclear in 2024 and Juliebø serves as chief commercial officer.

Emerald Nuclear has signed a lease for an engineering center in Norway, where it’s designing and building its first prototype, a non-nuclear thermal device that will be used for the Marine Nuclear Propulsion System Pilot project.

Other partners for the project are VARD Group, Vard Electro, Island Offshore, Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Imperial College London and Maskindynamikk, bringing together nuclear technology, ship design and integration, vessel operations and academic research.

The startup will build its first nuclear reactor , named the Gem Microreactor, at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology, with 2030 as its goal for completion. Emerald Nuclear will integrate equipment from Peregrine Turbine Technologies in Maine to convert the reactor’s heat into electricity.
The target for the first commercial deployment is 2031, on a Norwegian offshore vessel.

Deason is hoping to open a manufacturing site in the future in Western Washington on Puget Sound with an initial focus on floating nuclear power systems that replace diesel generators. That phase of growth is roughly targeted to the early 2030s.

articles.title: Who’s getting Anthropic’s compute spending? IPO filing shows where the tech giants really stand
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Anthropic’s IPO filing reads like a ledger of who’s getting paid in the AI boom. The Seattle region’s tech giants are on the list, but they aren’t at the top.

The prospectus, filed Monday with the Securities and Exchange Commission, details more than $750 billion in computing deals, including firm commitments and estimated future spending, and offers clues about what its founders and biggest investors stand to gain ahead of the company’s planned Nasdaq listing under the ticker ANT.

Amazon and Microsoft have invested billions in Anthropic and won high-profile spending commitments from the Claude maker. But both trail Google, chipmaker Broadcom and Elon Musk’s SpaceX in their shares of Anthropic’s planned spending on computing power, the filing shows.

Following the compute money: Google’s chips are the biggest winner. Anthropic has lined up roughly $400 billion in computing capacity, mostly over the next seven years, based on Google-designed AI chips, known as tensor processing units or TPUs.

That total includes $114.5 billion to Google directly through July 2033, $161.2 billion in equipment leases with chipmaker Broadcom, and an estimated $125 billion to $150 billion in additional TPU capacity from 2028 to 2031.
Broadcom’s leases are the largest single arrangement in the filing. The five-year leases provide TPU-based hardware for data centers operated by other companies on Anthropic’s behalf.
Elon Musk’s SpaceX is next. Anthropic agreed to spend up to $120.5 billion through 2029 for computing capacity from SpaceX’s AI subsidiary, formerly known as xAI, which runs a rival AI lab.

The filing says payments will reach about $3.1 billion a month once all the capacity is delivered, which Anthropic expects in December. The agreements run into 2029, though either side can cancel on 90 days’ notice after early 2027.

Amazon is still a big winner. Anthropic committed in April to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon Web Services over 10 years, through April 2036, and AWS Trainium is one of four chip families that Anthropic uses to train and run its models.
Microsoft’s piece is smaller, which reflects its later start. The company was aligned closely with OpenAI for years before striking its own deal with Anthropic .

Anthropic has committed to spend at least $44.9 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud from November 2026 through May 2033, the filing shows. That’s up from the $30 billion Azure deal announced in November 2025. The deal has been amended twice since, most recently this month.
Claude is built into Microsoft 365 , and former Microsoft CFO Chris Liddell joined Anthropic’s board in February.

Two smaller providers have deals in the same range as Microsoft’s. Anthropic agreed to spend up to about $44.6 billion with Nscale, a U.K.-based AI infrastructure company, and about $41.3 billion with GPU cloud provider Lambda, both for capacity powered by Nvidia chips, according to the filing.
Will Anthropic need it all? Most of the commitments can’t be canceled, and the deals with Microsoft, Google and Amazon require Anthropic to pay “regardless of actual usage,” according to the filing.

So far, the demand is there. Anthropic’s revenue hit $11.6 billion in the second quarter, up from $787 million a year earlier, and the company posted its first operating profit, $974 million. It still had a $66.3 billion net loss, mostly from accounting charges tied to its soaring valuation.
The company says it has “consistently operated in a compute-constrained environment where customer demand exceeds available compute.”

Its compute commitments assume that demand keeps growing. Anthropic spent less than $2 billion a month on compute and infrastructure in the second quarter. The SpaceX deal alone is expected to cost about $3.1 billion a month at full capacity.

Paper fortunes: Amazon’s biggest payoff is its stake , which it valued at $190.4 billion as of June 30 in its quarterly SEC filing . That includes convertible notes with $6.2 billion in principal that Amazon valued at $97.9 billion. The notes would convert into stock, subject to a 12% ownership cap that Amazon can waive.

Amazon is scheduled to report third-quarter results Thursday, its first earnings report since Anthropic’s filing. The Seattle-based company has updated the value of its Anthropic holdings in each of its quarterly filings this year, so a new number could come this week.

Google put $10 billion into Anthropic’s latest funding round and can invest up to $20 billion more under a March financing deal. The filing doesn’t give ownership percentages for Amazon, Google or Microsoft. It says only that the three companies have each made “significant equity investments” in Anthropic.

Anthropic’s seven co-founders hold roughly 230 million to 245 million shares each, worth about $14 billion apiece at the latest private funding price. The company also gave its own Public Benefit Fund about 847 million shares, or 5% of its fully diluted stock as of June 30, worth about $50 billion at that price.

Anthropic could begin formally marketing its IPO to investors as soon as the week of Nov. 9, Bloomberg reported , citing people familiar with the matter. It is aiming to go public the following week, according to the Wall Street Journal . The company expects the offering to match or beat the size of SpaceX’s IPO, according to Bloomberg. SpaceX raised $75 billion in June , the largest IPO on record.

articles.title: AI optimism meets data center backlash as protesters disrupt Seattle AI Week kickoff
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: The Washington Technology Industry Association kicked off the third annual Seattle AI Week on Monday with a reminder that AI affects everyone, from engineers and artists to “someone who learned about ChatGPT today,” as WTIA’s Nick Ellingson put it.
“All of us should be a part of that conversation,” he added.
A few people in the audience took that statement literally.

Members of Troublemakers , a Seattle climate activism group, interrupted the week’s opening panel on AI and economic growth several times before they were led out by security. Outside on Elliott Bay, others floated in kayaks with a banner: “Power for People, Not for Tech.”

“These are not your constituents — we are,” one protester told Beau Perschbacher , Gov. Bob Ferguson’s senior policy advisor, as he addressed the large crowd of tech and startup leaders at Seattle’s AI House . Perschbacher was on a panel with Joe Nguyen of the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce and Mattie Zazueta of OpenAI, the event’s presenting sponsor.

The group’s main message, according to members who spoke with GeekWire: the rush to build data centers and roll out AI is putting the state’s communities, jobs and environment at risk, and Washington should be investing in green jobs and clean energy instead.

The protest comes amid a broader backlash against data centers in Washington state and across the country. The Seattle City Council voted unanimously in June to pause new large data centers in the city for a year, and Washington AI Resistance organized at least 19 protests around the state this month calling for a statewide moratorium.

The event also came the same day Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, roughly a quarter of its workforce, as it spends tens of billions of dollars on data centers and AI infrastructure.
The backlash contrasts with a push from the business and tech community for Washington state and the Seattle region to do more to stay competitive in the AI era.

“Washington helped build the technology economy of the last generation. We have an extraordinary opportunity to lead the AI economy of the next,” said former Gov. Chris Gregoire, now CEO of the business group Challenge Seattle, in her opening remarks at the AI Week event.

Gregoire cited efforts to put AI to work on the region’s own problems, including an AI permitting pilot in Everett that she said could cut the median wait for an accessory dwelling unit permit from 252 days to 90. She highlighted the AI-driven protein design work of Nobel laureate David Baker of the University of Washington, with applications in areas including the environment, agriculture and health care.
She also warned that Washington is close to the bottom for its business climate, even though it ranks second in North America for tech talent, as other states court its companies and jobs.

On the panel, Perschbacher said Ferguson’s administration has been focused on data centers since taking office, setting up a work group early last year to study their impact. The group looked for a Washington community that had been harmed by a data center and couldn’t find one, he said.
He added that the state won’t permit data centers to run diesel generators around the clock, and that their water use turned out to be “not out of line with a typical industrial user.”

Electricity is a different story. Data centers “use a really significant amount of electricity,” he said, and with demand also rising from EVs and heat pumps, getting enough power “is a major challenge.”

Perschbacher addressed the protesters directly, saying Washington has some of the strictest environmental laws in the country and that the state’s data center work group reinforced those rules rather than weakening them. Bills on ratepayer protections and transparency for data centers are likely to come back in the next legislative session, he said.

The issue also came up in the event’s second panel, on AI policy. State Sen. Marko Liias , who sponsored a bill this year on high-risk uses of AI, said data centers that want to locate in Washington need to meet “stringent expectations,” including adding clean energy to the grid, recycling water and dropping nondisclosure agreements that keep communities in the dark. Washington’s goal “has never been to be the cheapest or easiest place,” he said.
“When energy becomes scarce, I do think we need to be clear that our communities deserve access to that energy before the data centers do,” Liias said.

Joe Braidwood , founder of AI governance startup Glacis , which works out of AI House, said on the same panel that it was the first event he’d attended there with a public protest. “I think that’s actually kind of promising that people care enough to want to come together and talk and disagree and figure this out,” he said.

Zazueta, OpenAI’s global head of community programs, said in the opening panel that the industry needs to do a better job showing people the benefits of AI. Many people “read about these scary headlines,” she said, but don’t see how the technology applies to their daily lives.

OpenAI runs AI literacy workshops and trains libraries and community groups to lead their own, she said. The company opened an expanded office in Bellevue in March, its largest engineering center outside San Francisco.

Speaking with GeekWire outside the event on Monday afternoon, one of the protesters who had interrupted the panel singled out that remark. She said it dismissed public concerns about AI as the product of bad headlines, and she objected to the idea of using community groups to win people over to the benefits of artificial intelligence.
“They want to infiltrate our communities,” she said.

The opening panel with Zazueta, Perschbacher and Nguyen was titled “The Abundance State: Washington’s Chance to Lead the AI Future.” The protester objected to that framing, saying the panelists’ idea of abundance came down to easing permits for data centers.

It wasn’t the first time the group has protested the tech industry’s energy use. In 2024, it blocked entrances at Amazon’s Seattle headquarters to protest the company’s plans to power data centers in Oregon with natural gas.

Inside the event on Monday, as the interruptions continued, Nguyen, a former state senator who now leads the Seattle chamber, had responded to the protesters directly. “If you want to have your own event, have your own event,” he told them.

After they were led out, Nguyen said he agreed with the protesters, calling their passion “very warranted.” Those concerns are one reason Washington created some of the most stringent energy policies in the country, he said, adding that everyone would be better off if data centers elsewhere were held to the same standards.
“I think we’re very unique in Washington state to be able to actually do this in a way that really is mindful of our values, of the environment, and also pushing for innovation as well,” he said.
At the same time, Nguyen said demand for AI and data centers is market-driven, and it isn’t fair to criticize data centers while using them every day.
“For anybody who’s upset with data centers, I hope that when you email me, don’t email me,” he said. “Print it off and walk it to my office.”

Update, Oct. 27: Protesters interrupted the opening session of WTIA’s Seattle AI Summit six times Tuesday morning, during an on-stage interview of OpenAI’s Vijaye Raji by GeekWire’s Todd Bishop. They objected to AI-related job losses, the climate impact of data centers, OpenAI’s ties to the Trump administration and the leadership of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

articles.title: Op-Ed: The Case for Public Access at University Swimming Pools
articles.author: Collin Reid
paras: What is the community function of a university? Beyond employment, labs, and lecture halls, one underappreciated tertiary benefit is maintaining a walkable urban ecosystem as a model for urban design. For many Americans raised in the sprawling suburbs, university is the first and last time they live in a walkable community. Although universities possess neither the political nor material resources to reshape the entire national urban ecosystem, they can – and sometimes do – enhance their local communities by opening their recreational facilities to the public.

Pools are just one example of where universities could make a significant material contribution to their urban ecosystems. While opening both pools and fitness centers would be ideal, as universities could use the revenue generated to supplement student fees and theoretically decrease the cost of education, the community impact of a new pool would be far more significant.

This is because commercial fitness centers are significantly less capital intensive than pools, costing a few hundred thousand dollars to open, with the most basic facilities costing below $100,000 and only the largest most advanced facilities breaking into the millions. On the other hand, indoor commercial pools typically run into the tens of millions , and that’s before land acquisition.

The city of Shoreline is currently providing a pertinent insight into the financial cost and community value of a centrally located public pool. The city has placed Proposition 1 on this November’s ballot, where residents will vote on the construction of an aquatics facility to replace the one it closed in 2020 with an estimated cost of $100 million factoring in projected inflation by 2028 and 15% design contingencies. The design includes a leisure pool with a lazy river, a hot tub alongside a sauna, and an eight-lane 25-yard lap pool with diving boards.

Located in the heart of Shoreline at Midvale and 178th Street, the proposed pool will be within walking distance of the E, Route 333, and 348 bus lines, Shorewood High School, and multiple supermarkets. Successful passage would triple the year-round pool space open to the public in Shoreline, as the Dale Turner YMCA has a four-lane lap pool and a smaller leisure pool, and allow residents the opportunity to swim for a lower price while supporting their local government.

Pools are so expensive because the engineering behind them is complex: you don’t need precision angling of cement to plop some mats, barbells, and workout machines in a basic gym. The solution to increasing their availability isn’t to ignore regulations, but to recognize that the cheapest infrastructure is that which already exists. Evergreen Aquatics Center recognized this, opting to save a facility from demolition back in 2009, which saved the public tens of millions in financial and community value.

For the purposes of quantification, I’ll evaluate the ability of pools to serve lap swimming while acknowledging that pools can serve a wide variety of functions of varying capacities. All the publicly accessible indoor pools in Seattle have 79 lap lanes in total. Each lane can host eight swimmers (though I personally think sharing a lane with more than four people feels crowded), so all the publicly available pools in Seattle can host 632 lap swimmers at once at maximum capacity (316 comfortably).

All the public pools in Seattle have six lanes, and they offer the majority of space in this calculation. However, it is exceedingly rare that all lanes are open at public pools, especially in the afternoon when they have to balance demand with swimming lessons and other activities. This generally results in about one to two hours of lap swim available in the afternoon. By opening University of Washington’s 14-lane IMA pool and University of Seattle’s two six-lane pools for even just two hours of public lap swimming, these institutions would effectively add more than four public pools’ worth of lanes, absorbing demand to relieve crowding at public pools and potentially opening time and space to expand the variety of activities available.

In explaining why University of Washington’s pool isn’t open to the public, Assistant Director of Operations for Recreation, Chad Yarbrough, pointed to deference to tuition-paying students who fund the facility: “The IMA (Student Recreation Center) is not open to the general public because of space limitations and because access to the facility is funded through fees paid by UW students as part of their tuition.”
When asked whether the university had considered opening to the public before, he confirmed they had: “Yes. We have discussed these options before, however, [we] are not going in that direction.”

Seattle University was more amenable to the idea of public access, as they already partner with local swim teams who rent their facility on a regular basis. Assistant Director of UREC, Melissa Wessel, explained that the pools are currently closed to the wider public because “we don't have an easy way for folks who aren't a part of a specific group or UREC members to currently swim as building-wide access could be an issue. We are currently exploring more ways to better serve the Seattle swim community.”

Along with relieving demand for public pools, UW and Seattle U could also enhance the walkability and bikeability of the urban ecosystem. Seattle U’s central location in a relatively dense urban area could pedestrianize a number of trips, and University of Washington’s pool is about a quarter mile from the Link station bearing the public institution’s name. From a transit perspective, University of Washington’s pool would further capitalize upon the apparent decision to prioritize traffic flows to stadiums when designing the Link and planning bus lines.

Because Seattle already hosts a decent amount of public and private pools accessible via transit throughout the city, opening university pools to the public would most likely relieve demand for lap swimming at public pools while integrating more people into the community spirits they already engender among alumni and with other programs. This is particularly true for Seattle U, where there are two YMCA pools and the public Medgar Evers pool all located close by and easily accessed via transit. It’s outside of Seattle, in cities like Tacoma and Bellingham, where universities like Puget Sound, Pacific Lutheran, and Western Washington have the potential to make the greatest impact on their local communities.

Like Seattle U, University of Puget Sound (UPS) has options for people to swim somewhat nearby and is somewhat accessible via transit. However, as central Tacoma has only two bus routes of 30-60 minute frequency that both primarily feed into downtown (the 11 and the 16), this leaves the area significantly car dependent. However, the Pierce County bus expansions contained within Proposition 1 on the ballot this November offer the opportunity to greatly boost service, if it passes.

UPS’s eight-lane pool would significantly contribute to the walkability and usefulness of transit to its surrounding area if it opened to the public. With more frequent transit and a proper north-south route along Union Avenue or Alder Street, the greenspace and facilities of UPS would have even more potential to serve as a walkable and transit-oriented community hub, decreasing car dependency and generating a more localized sense of place. Unfortunately, UPS didn’t respond to my inquiries, and there is no evidence that they have any plans to capitalize upon their potential in this regard.

Further south, technically south of Tacoma, lies the Census Designated Place of Parkland, a former streetcar suburb with Pacific Lutheran University (PLU) right at its heart and along the (in)famous Route 1 down Pacific Avenue, Pierce County’s most used bus route, which ironically had once had rails. Pacific Avenue has become a prototypical sprawl-based stroad in the decades since the rails were torn away all while the area has been suffering from poverty, violence, and neglect from the government. The poverty and violence have created a stigma about the area that can cause people to write it off, and a somewhat recent example of this neglect arose with the now abandoned bus rapid transit (BRT) system to serve Pacific Avenue.

The people of Parkland do not deserve this stigma and neglect, and PLU’s location at the community’s heart places it in a perfect position to pump vibrancy back into the area if it allows the people to circulate through its system.

To its credit, PLU has taken steps to offer services to the community and begin the process of serving as a hub: the public can and does utilize its beautiful greenspaces, it plans to open a medical clinic in partnership with MultiCare , and they offer free tutoring and English Language Learning (ELL) classes at the Parkland Literacy Center. These are all good starts, especially if the clinic offers free or at least discounted services to members of the community regardless of whether they meet the strict requirements for Medicare.
When it comes to PLU’s pool, the institution has taken some very small steps by hosting affordable public swim lessons, but remains committed to keeping the pool closed to the public beyond that.

“Because the pool’s operations are funded directly by student tuition, our schedule must prioritize the intensive demands of our varsity athletic programs, student intramurals, and campus recreation," PLU’s director of digital communications Christopher Albert said. "We do not offer general public open-swim hours to ensure our students have full access to the resources essential to their collegiate experience, while keeping our public engagement focused on high-value safety programs.”

Though swimming lessons are useful, is there not a certain irony to teaching people how to swim and then not offering any window of time, however brief, to use the only lap pool in their community? The pool’s location within walking distance of Keithley Middle School, Washington High School, and blocks upon blocks of residential housing has the potential to serve as a meaningful third space, even if open to the public for only a couple hours a week, and would synergize with the steps the university is taking towards community integration. If the issue is funding, even a small membership fee would go a long way with sustained public participation.

Examining the greater Tacoma region as a whole, the physical distribution of UPS and PLU are more significant than the number of lanes they would increase. Large sections of residential suburban housing across the region are severely underserved by public transportation, which leaves room for the universities to pedestrianize pool trips for the communities immediately surrounding. For both PLU and UPS, this might mean that a few limited hours with a membership fee would both ensure their facilities aren’t overstrained and provide funding to supplement student fees that support the pool.

Western Washington University (WWU) in Bellingham represents a moderated synthesis of the potential for universities in Seattle by increasing the lane capacity of the entire city, and in greater Tacoma, by serving as pedestrian neighborhood hubs.

Bellingham only has 16 pool lanes open to the public, and none of them are publicly owned. This means that WWU opening its pool to the public would offer the greatest relative increase in number of lanes in its community (unless we count Parkland as its own community) and provide swimming opportunities beyond the private business sector, as WWU is a public institution.

At the immediate neighborhood level, WWU’s pool opening to the public could have similar effects at pedestrianizing trips as UPS and PLU would. The main issue is that unlike the grid patterns surrounding UPS and PLU, the streets surrounding WWU are elongated with few intersections, requiring pedestrians to cut across private property for the quickest route.

The bus routes connecting to WWU also already feed into the downtown Bellingham core where pools already exist, so locals around the university would most practically cycle to the pool rather than walk or take transit. One might consider it a tertiary benefit: residents would get the benefit of a light warmup and cooldown exercise.

So what value can we attach to this contribution? Shoreline is suggesting $100 million for its new eight-lane complex with extra amenities, but this includes a non-lap pool, Jacuzzi, saunas, etc. Let’s say we say the lap pool represents a third of the value of that facility: that’s $33 million for eight lanes, a little more than $4 million per lane. As those lanes are going to be used by the public exclusively whereas university pools would require limited hours to accommodate swim teams, let’s shave that down even more to just $500,000 per lane.

At that rate, UW and Seattle U opening their pools to the public even in a limited capacity would still represent a $13 million capital improvement to the community. UPS and PLU $7 million, and WWU $3 million. This represents an extremely conservative estimate, as public pool facilities regularly cost tens of millions of dollars, and it’s all money that communities would not have to spend if these universities provided a means for the public to access their facilities even in a limited capacity that accommodates student athletics.

What about value beyond dollar figures, for those of us who aren’t neoliberal capitalists? Pools serve as a vital third space that uniquely combines relaxation and fitness to all ages and nearly all levels of ability: after work or school people can unwind in isolation by swimming laps or building community in group activities. It’s also a place to develop swimming skills which save people’s lives .

By opening their pools to the public, these universities would allow more areas to become walkable, enjoyable, and safer all while more fully integrating themselves into their surrounding communities. These are the types of broad social goals administrators at these institutions constantly profess, and they should feel fortunate that they have the opportunity to realize them so easily in this instance.

articles.title: How the Federal Way Link Extension Impacted Bus Ridership Patterns
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: In December 2025, Sound Transit welcomed the first passengers aboard the Federal Way Link Extension. The three new stations on the 1 Line provide improved transit connectivity for many south King County residents. An accompanying bus service change in March 2026 improved frequency on many bus routes and adjusted a few bus routes to better connect with the new Link stations. While some routes lost ridership, many other routes welcomed new passengers. Link increased the total number of transit trips in south King County with nearly 10,000 combined weekday boardings at Federal Way, Star Lake, and Kent Des Moines stations.

This article will discuss the stop-level ridership data for select routes in south King County. To minimize the impact of seasonal changes in ridership, the analysis compares data from March-August 2025 with data from March-August 2026. The plots below show average weekday boardings and alightings at each stop, boardings are shown with positive bars, alightings are shown with negative bars. The different colors represent the number of passengers boarding/alighting during that time of day. The data for 2025 is shown as slightly faded. Click on each plot to open it in a new tab.

Route 181 serves as the primary east-west route between Federal Way and Auburn. Federal Way Transit Center has long been a busy stop as it connects passengers with many other bus routes. The new Federal Way Link station caused a 46% increase in Route 181 boardings at that stop each day, from 293 to 430 passengers. Overall ridership on Route 181 increased by about 114 passengers and the ridership at other stops was not significantly impacted.

Route 183 is a coverage route between Federal Way and Kent, via the new Star Lake station. Prior to the Federal Way Link Extension, the route connected to freeway bus routes 177, 193, and 574 at I-5 & 272nd St. That connection generated about 4 boardings per day for Route 183. Now, 71 passengers board Route 183 each weekday at Star Lake station, a 1,675% increase. This is still just a fraction of the 1,600 weekday Link boardings at the station as many Link passengers use the station’s 1,100 space parking garage. Both of the route’s termini, Federal Way and Kent, have a slight decrease in ridership. This may be from some passengers switching to Link at Star Lake rather than to another bus in Federal Way or Kent.

The A Line now runs in the 1 Line’s shadow between Federal Way and Tukwila. Thanks to fast and frequent service along Pacific Hwy, it was the most productive Metro route in 2024 . Now that Link offers a faster trip north from Federal Way, this title may be in trouble. Stops across the A Line have reduced ridership from 2025. At Federal Way Transit Center, boardings on the A Line have dropped 19%. Likewise, the number of passengers boarding the A Line at Pacific Hwy & 240th St (near Kent Des Moines station) has been cut in half. Part of this severe drop in boardings is due to the new A Line stop that opened next to Kent Des Moines station. When factoring in boardings at that stop, there is still a 24% decrease in A Line boardings near Kent Des Moines station. A similar change occurred at International Blvd & 200th St, next to Angle Lake station. Many passengers who previously rode the A Line to the Link 1 Line’s southern terminus in 2025 are now opting to board Link at one of the new stations. Despite this drop in ridership, the A Line still provides critical local service along Pacific Hwy. As the area continues to develop, ridership on the A Line will rebound.

Route 165 connected Burien and Des Moines with Kent and Auburn via the newly opened Kent Des Moines Link station. Since the new station opened, boardings on Route 165 at the nearby stops (Pacific Hwy & KDM Rd, KDM Station, Pacific Hwy & 240th St) have increased 50% (109 daily passengers). This increase is offset by 70 fewer boardings at Kent Sounder Station, suggesting some passengers have switched from Sounder to Link. The route’s termini both have slightly reduced boarding counts as well, likely also due to the new station. For instance, someone traveling between Normandy Park and downtown Seattle may have switched from the 165 + H Line to 165 + 1 Line for their trip. In August 2026, Route 165 was replaced by routes 164 and 166.

The Federal Way Link Extension also impacted a few Sound Transit Express bus routes. As these routes are operated by Pierce Transit, we do not have detailed ridership data for them (yet). Instead, this analysis will use the overall route ridership comparing April 2025 to April 2026.

Ridership on Route 574 increased about 10% year-over-year. This is mostly from more people traveling between Lakewood or Tacoma and Link in Federal Way. Route 574 previously connected with Link at SeaTac, so the FWLE likely did not attract too many new passengers. The August 2026 service change truncated Route 574 at Federal Way in exchange for a much needed frequency boost, which should further increase ridership.

Routes 577 and 578 form the primary bus connection between downtown Seattle and Federal Way. Most times of the day, these routes are still faster than Link for that trip. As a result, ridership has not changed too dramatically. Boardings are down 10% on both routes. Routes 577 and 578 both saw a more significant drop in ridership immediately after the FWLE opening in December, but ridership has since rebounded. Whether the recent ridership increases are due to the routes’ lower travel time or due to the World Cup and other seasonal ridership changes is still up in the air.

The Federal Way Link Extension is already making its mark on travel patterns in south King County. Local routes connecting with Link are busier than last year. Meanwhile, ST Express routes and the RapidRide A Line lost some passengers to Link. The August 2026 service change further improved local connectivity in south King County that should make transit the best option for even more trips.

While this article only covered a few routes, detailed ridership data for most King County Metro routes is now updated at seattletransitridership.com . In addition, the impact of the Crosslake Connection on bus routes in east King County was discussed in a recent article .

articles.title: A new climb: Capitol Hill’s Annapurna Cafe gets an early start on its plan to move up Broadway
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: For its trek to the top of Seattle process to create a new, updated home for the beloved Himalayan joint, Broadway’s Annapurna Cafe is starting early.
Late this summer, Annapurna’s owners filed permit paperwork to begin buildout on a brand new Broadway space for the restaurant — work they don’t expect to start until next November.
“We heard that the City of Seattle is really behind for improvement approval,” Sujan Sharma tells CHS about the paperwork.

While Sharma and Roshita Shrestha continue to serve their much-loved thalis, curries, and breads in its underground space below the old Crest Building at 1833 Broadway, Annapurna is being prepared for a climb north.

A few years back, Sharma and Shrestha purchased a Broadway commercial condo on the street level of the Brix building near a few doors down from Vivace . The corner was the long ago home of Dilettante Mocha Café . The couple have leased the space to Star Sushi in recent years.
Plans are now in motion for it become Annapurna’s new home.

Working with Nos Narin , the design director at Catch Design Studio behind many Capitol Hill food and drink overhauls, the space is being planned for a full upgrade including an overhaul of the kitchen, plus a redesign of the interior — once the city finally signs off on the plans over the coming months.

The new start for Annapurna will come after more than 20 years on Broadway. Shrestha and Sharma started Annapurna in May 2003 as a small venture to introduce the cuisine to Broadway and the Capitol Hill neighborhood. Shrestha said that she wanted to bring flavors that she had grown up with to Seattle. Challenges around the pandemic and the years of construction for the Capitol Hill Light Rail Station and its next door west-side entrance nearly did the restaurant in. But Annapurna persevered — and expanded. In 2015, it reached the surface on Broadway, adding its upstairs Yeti Bar above the lower level Broadway restaurant.
Any redevelopment at 1833 Broadway will need a new, landmarks-friendly design

As for the 1905-built-building the restaurant currently calls home, it has long been lined up for redevelopment as a six-story, 50-unit mixed-use building under plans first approved a decade ago . That project was put on ice due to landmarks protections . Any new development plan will need to incorporate preservation of the building’s historic proportions, look, and feel.
The extra time has given Annapurna time to prepare and, along the way, learn a few lessons about Seattle process including the most important — start early.
Annapurna Cafe is still located at 1833 Broadway. Learn more at annapurnacafe.com .

articles.title: Separation of assets: Thieves beat ex, take $10K and Bitcoin-stuffed tablet in Capitol Hill heist
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Police say an early-morning apartment robbery on Capitol Hill netted a pair of thieves $10,000 in cash and a tablet tied to nearly $250,000 in cryptocurrency — a target the victim said was likely exposed after his estranged wife bragged about his finances to online acquaintances.

According to a Seattle Police Department incident report, officers were dispatched last Wednesday to a Capitol Hill apartment. The victim reported waking up around 4:00 AM to discover an unfamiliar man and woman stealing $10,000 in cash along with a tablet computer.
The victim told police the tablet held access to digital wallets containing 3.0 Bitcoins, valued at roughly $246,621, and 42.0 PI Network tokens worth about $3.30.

When the victim confronted the intruders, the male suspect punched him, and the woman brandished a knife. The victim pursued the pair outside toward Capitol Hill Station where he was punched again, shoved into a bush, and suffered a broken nose before the suspects escaped eastbound on E John in a black Dodge sedan.

Whether the thieves drove away with a quarter-million dollars or just a locked tablet is not clear. While the paper cash was gone immediately, moving cryptocurrency off a stolen device is not easy. Without passcodes, private recovery keys, or account logins, the suspects cannot access the funds—and if the victim still has those keys, he can simply transfer the digital money to a safe account before anyone unlocks the device.
The SPD report did not provide further details about the status of the victim’s cryptocurrency.

The victim told police that he believed his estranged wife had invited the pair into the apartment. While the victim maintained she was not complicit in the robbery, he believed her drinking and open boasting about his wealth prompted her social media acquaintances to target the booty.
According to the report, police may have encountered the suspects during a related contact earlier that day.

articles.title: Seattle Council opens budget debate with little room for district priorities including Hollingsworth’s $2.5M Central District-South Seattle fund
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Hollingsworth’s latest social media update lays out her priorities this budget amendment season

When it comes to the rosters of budget amendments earmarked for spending in their own districts, the Seattle City Council is facing a more challenging political environment this year. District 3 representative and Council President Joy Hollingsworth is facing the same difficult financial landscape as she pushes her proposed 2027-2028 budget updates forward including a plan to boost the economy in the Central District and another that could help fund the revival of neighborhood councils in Seattle.

The Seattle City Council is digging into budget deliberations Tuesday, opening the first of three days of debate over member-sponsored amendments to Mayor Katie Wilson’s 2027–2028 budget proposal and plan to wipe out a $175 million city deficit.

Between Tuesday and Thursday, councilmembers will review dozens of Council Budget Actions and Statements of Legislative Intent across City Hall before budget committee chair Dan Strauss unveils his balancing package next week.

Tuesday’s opening budget committee session addressed 16 departments including the City Attorney’s office, civil rights, the Office of Housing, the Department of Neighborhoods, planning, finance, and infrastructure utility departments.

With the focus on eliminating the deficit without cutting vital services, councilmembers are describing a limited playing field with little room for maneuvering or negotiation and are buttressing their district and neighborhood needs as part of wider citywide programs.
Hollingsworth’s roster of amendments focused on neighborhood reinvestment, tenant protection, and civic participation is a good example.

Leading the package is Hollingsworth’s proposal, co-sponsored by Rob Saka and Dionne Foster , which earmarks $2.5 million annually alongside two full-time equivalent positions to launch a Central District and Southeast Seattle Reinvestment Program . The Hollingsworth-led initiative would establish a grant process to deliver operational funding to community organizations as part of investments across the city’s southern core.

Additionally, Hollingsworth partnered with Debora Juarez and Bob Kettle on a budget action proposing $100,000 annually to support a revival of Seattle neighborhood councils. The spending comes a decade after the city removed much of its support for a former neighborhood council system over concerns the groups did not fully represent their communities.

Hollingsworth is also leading a measure adding $500,000 in support to the Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections to lift the city’s baseline tenant services budget to $3 million in 2027 for eviction defense, legal representation, and renter education.

Other headline amendments from the first session targeted court backlogs, affordable housing, and urban land use. Councilmembers proposed a coordinated push for the City Attorney’s Office to address a backlog of roughly 5,000 misdemeanor cases — a third of which involve domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, or elder abuse — by proposing $1 million in flexible 2027 relief funds, $1.28 million to hire four assistant city prosecutors, and $277,000 annually to contract out toxicology testing under state law.

On the housing front, Foster introduced a $10 million appropriation for rental and homeownership units in 2027 alongside companion legislation requiring unspent JumpStart Payroll Expense Tax balances to automatically roll over year-to-year, a move hoped to counter the mayor’s proposal to cut $65 million from the 2026 Office of Housing budget.

Other key proposals include a $3 million plan by Alexis Mercedes Rinck to fund a public market in Highland Park, an ordinance to divert at least 70% of new “Do Not Solicit” penalties toward anti-displacement legal and home repair assistance for homeowners, an assessment on building affordable housing at SPU’s newly acquired 18-acre Yesler Creek site, and a formal scoping study to examine lidding I-5 near the new Pinehurst light rail station .

Deliberations continue Wednesday with presentations turning to Seattle Parks , the Seattle Department of Transportation and the Seattle Fire Department where a debate over a proposed cut to firefighter overtime is likely to be a center of the session.

Thursday’s session will include the Seattle Police Department as councilmembers take on questions around spending on police hiring in the mayor’s plan that calls for capping the department at 1,250 officers as part of measures to cut the forecast deficit.

CHS reported here on Wilson’s full budget proposal which would wipe out an inherited $175 million deficit without tax increases or withdrawals from city reserves. The proposal would cut roughly $50 million annually in General Fund spending by eliminating 128 positions and adjusting a department’s projected funding to what it has spent in recent years, pairing these cuts with $50 million in shuffled funding — primarily leveraging JumpStart payroll tax revenues to cover core services and homelessness programs — and enabling the city, Wilson says, to project balanced budgets through 2030 without drawing on reserves.
The plan requires compromises along the edges on things like firefighter overtime and hiring new cops — unless the council’s amendment process digs up ways to cover the costs.

articles.author: Dan Savage
paras: I’m a 45-year-old single gay cis man out there in the world. I met a 50-year-old cis married man on Grindr. We had hot sex and have been hitting it off ever since. Here’s the problem: I was under the impression at first that he and his wife practiced some form of ENM or had some version of a “Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell” agreement. At this point, however, I know that all the man-on-man sex he’s having with me and others is just old-fashioned cheating. Among other pieces of evidence that he’s cheating: He’s having his PrEP and DoxyPEP mailed to my address (good on him for being proactive about this) and he goes out of his way to cover his tracks in other ways. More context: His spouse is the breadwinner and he stays at home. Housework is work, of course, and he does the housework, but he has no income. They’ve been married for more than 25 years and they haven’t had sex of any kind in at least eighteen years. He jokes about maybe having a sex addiction and is also a little smug about getting away with fucking whoever he wants, whenever he wants. Do you think the wife should be tipped off to what he’s doing? She is going to find out eventually… I’m certain of that. Also, he’s got a teenage son who is gay and out and he can’t seem to see the problem of his being in the closet while his son is out.
Is this guy a lost cause? Should I cut ties? Or is there a way forward?

You clearly wanna tell this guy’s wife he’s been cheating on her — I’m getting subtle “aggrieved mistress” vibes from your question — but I don’t think you’ll be telling his wife anything she doesn’t already know. She may not know her husband is bisexual and fucking you and God only knows how many other men, CHEAT, but she most likely assumes he hasn’t been celibate for the last eighteen years.

That said, being confronted with the proof — of his cheating and his bisexuality — could cause this woman pain, CHEAT. For all you know, he’s the reason their marriage is sexless and she has lived every day for nearly two decades with the sting of her husband’s sexual rejection. So, why does she stay? Well, sometimes a person is able to limp along in a sexless marriage because they believe the sexual deprivation is mutual — they believe this misery is a load they share — but finding out your spouse is out there taking loads while you read the books and make the appointments … yeah, this guy’s wife could go from resigned and content to wounded and devastated before she finishes reading your email.

But maybe everything this guy has told you about his marriage is true — always a big leap when a married person wants to get into your pants — and his wife is one of those women who doesn’t wanna fuck her husband but won’t give her husband permission to fuck anyone else. If that’s the case, then your lover is only guilty of doing what he needs to do to stay married and stay sane. And if there are good reasons why they stay together — financial dependence is one reason people stay, CHEAT, but so is emotional/social dependence — then your email could wind up doing more harm than good.

Look, you’re free to find it sad that this man isn’t out to his wife or his gay kid, CHEAT, but I don’t think you have a right to blow up his life — his thoroughly compromised life — because you think it would be better for all involved (presumably yourself included) if he was out. It sounds like this guy is a bit of an asshole… and it sounds like you caught feelings for him at some point… and now you feel like you’ve been used. But outing a cheater for cheating when you’re done cheating with him (or he’s done cheating with you) is always a bad look.
P.S. If the “way forward” you’re imagining is some sort of future where you’re with this guy… yeah, maybe you tell him what you’re feeling instead of telling his wife what he’s been doing.

I am a 40-year-old cisgender bi woman living in the Midwest. I have a question about one of my best friends, a trans woman. I’ve known this person for over fifteen years, most of that before their transition. They grew up as a white man, middle class, and didn’t deal with any of the things that women deal with growing up. I’m referencing harassment and assault, especially with the recent case in the news of the students at Cornell University. This individual grew up to be a relatively successful man with a six-figure income, nice house, and a pretty average life. They came out as trans a few years ago and I’ve been incredibly supportive during their transition. The thing that I’m having trouble with is their newfound “feminism.” When we talk about the struggles women face, they speak as someone who has been through and lived through those experiences. As an AFAB woman who grew up in the 1990s and 2000s and has dealt with harassment and sexual assault, this is really upsetting to me. I absolutely love my friend, but it really hurts me when they claim to understand the plight of women in America when they have identified as a woman for less than three years. How can I bring this topic up without turning it into a major argument? Am I being too sensitive? Should I just agree with them and move on? I need help here.

I’m not a woman, TRA, but I do listen to women (when I remember to close my mouth) and I try not to talk over women (which is easier to do with my mouth closed). I like to think that all that listening has given me — a cis man — some understanding, however imperfect and incomplete, of what women face. So, it’s possible your friend… if she was listening before her transition… has some understanding herself.
But your annoyance with your friend, this recently hatched egg , is likewise understandable.

I’ve been out and gay for — OMG — more than forty years, TRA, and nothing annoys me more than having gayness explained to me by someone who has been out and gay for forty minutes. In some cases, these newly out guys are being thoughtless. But in others, TRA, the newly out guy isn’t talking to me. They’re not saying things I need to hear… they’re saying things they need to hear. But my M.O. is the same in both cases: I let them talk. Even if it means having to listen to someone who was born in 2002 explain to me just how bad things were for gay people in the 1980s, I let them talk. They either realize they’re being ridiculous (“I mean, I don’t need to tell you this!”) or they hear what they needed to hear and the conversation moves on to other things. (I do reserve the right to blow up when a newly out cis gay man tries to tell me that cis gay men played no role in the struggle for gay rights — we just partied, fucked, and died while nonbinary asexuals did the heavy lifting — or that the gay rights movement was hijacked in the 1990s by gay men who wanted to throw themselves wedding showers. Those are fighting words.)

So, my advice: Let your old friend run her mouth. Don’t argue, stare blankly, and change the subject when there’s a lull. Here’s hoping your friend, like those newly out gay boys, eventually gets this shit out of her system. But if she doesn’t — if she literally can’t stop explaining womanhood to you — feel free to spend less time with her.

articles.title: Inside the Gremlins Museum
articles.author: Audrey Vann
paras: “Where can I get a Gremlin?” was the question Ian Grant asked himself when he first saw the comedy-horror Christmas film at the drive-in back in 1984. “I was probably too young to see it,” he admitted. Although the film fueled nightmares of little green monsters under his bed, it also sparked a lifelong obsession (love and fear are closely related, after all).

It took nearly four decades for Grant to make his childhood dream a reality. He acquired a rare gremlin puppet from the first movie on eBay, and it was in rough condition—typical for other 35-year-old puppets. Grant worked with foam-latex restoration artists to repair his treasured prop back to form, while preserving its original elements. This was the start of the Gremlins Museum—a quaint office and hallway in Grant’s home—which now displays dozens of original props, puppets, scripts, and posters from Gremlins and Gremlins 2: The New Batch , as well as hundreds of pieces of merchandise from both films.

The giant screen-used Gizmo immediately took our breath away when we walked into the room. Crafted for the sequel , this large-scale animatronic puppet was used for close-up shots in the film and reportedly cost approximately $250,000 to produce. While as many as 20 little Gizmo puppets were created for the film, only one giant Gizmo (or as Grant calls it, the “hero puppet”) was made. “When I first got him, he kinda had a deer-in-headlights look to him,” Grant recalled. But during the restoration process, his wide-eyed facial expression was adjusted to make him look calmer, sweeter, and more like himself.

Beside the giant Gizmo are his normal-scale animatronic Mogwai buddies from Gremlins 2, including Mohawk, George, and Daffy. It can’t be overstated just how soft these guys looked. We asked repeatedly if Grant ever gives his puppets a pat on the head or a belly rub, but he stressed that they were far too fragile. However, he did confirm that Daffy was just as soft as he looks: “I had to touch him a little bit extra to get him situated on his stand.”
Owning and restoring these pieces of film history is a big job. These puppets were not made to last, and Grant reveals that if they are not maintained, they will essentially turn to dust.

“Everybody that owns foam latex stuff has this nightmare of waking up to foam dust everywhere,” he said as we gasped in horror. All the puppets at the Gremlins Museum are showcased and preserved in museum-quality glass boxes. “This is their safe place,” says Grant. “Nobody can hurt them in the box.”

Facing the Mogwai is Grant’s collection of Gremlins. He owns three gremlin puppets from the first movie and an original sculpt, which was used to create the puppets. While the Gremlins in the first film are fairly generic creatures, the sequel is a different story (perhaps you know, if you’ve seen the Key & Peele sketch ). The Gremlins in The New Batch are unique little monsters with names, personalities, and special abilities. Grant’s collection includes Bat Gremlin, Vegetable Gremlin, Lenny Gremlin, George Gremlin, Phantom Gremlin, “Out of Ammo” Gremlin (who shoots at John Wayne in a western scene which appears in an alternate VHS cut of the film), and most importantly, Greta Gremlin (aka the Girl Gremlin). Grant owns the “hero puppet” of Greta, meaning she was a functional animatronic and used in most of the movie scenes, as well as the sexy press pics. Grant notes that his puppet is the one used in the “iconic hand-on-hip” photo, which I, as a Greta stan, of course knew what photo he was talking about.

Other props in the museum include Gizmo’s pink Corvette, a Gremlin-used chainsaw, and a tiny gun (fired by a bandit Gremlin), all of which were used in the first film. Grant has acquired most of his props and puppets by becoming friends with folks who worked on the film and negotiating sales before they go on official auction markets. He noted that auctions are a losing game, considering that fees are high and that “there will always be someone with more money than you.” One of whom is Lord of the Rings director Peter Jackson, who is apparently also a Gremlins prop collector. “There was a big auction in 2022, and I went in hoping to get a bunch of stuff, but he came in and just killed everybody. I can’t compete with a billionaire.”

Since the museum is in Grant’s home, it is not open to the general public, but he welcomes a handful of passionate fans and media inquirers to take a peek at his collection. He also runs an extremely detailed online archive with virtual tours of the collection so that the creatures can be enjoyed by all. As of now, he has no current plans to expand the museum, but has considered contacting the Museum of Pop Culture to display the collection to the masses. However, the transportation of these fragile artifacts is a cause for concern. “It’s literally my nightmare…” he said with a laugh.

articles.title: Slog AM: Indiana ACLU Isn’t Thrilled With Nikkita Oliver’s Anti-Zionism, Washington Farmworkers Fight Bosses at the State Supreme Court, an Arsonist Targets der Führer

paras: Conservatives take power in British Columbia: The Tories haven’t held power in BC in around a century, though the province has been ruled by small-c conservatives in the meantime, like the Liberals and the dastardly Social Credit Party.
