Microsoft only expects around 3,000 of those employees to accept the buyouts. The announcement was good for the company’s short-term stock price, something management wants to hear considering first quarter financial reports are due tomorrow.

Seattle can’t stop liquidating children: What did all the prosperity from those tech jobs bring to Seattle? Not children. In fact, so few Seattleites can afford to raise children here that despite rampant, cancerous growth over the past decade and a half, the number of public school students has gone down—way down, to the point where we’re going to start closing schools, although school system administrators prefer the less alarming term “merging.” Details from KUOW. This exemplifies how the tech nouveau riches in our community represent not prosperity, but inequality.

Seattle cop who ordered officers to “fuck people up” for protesting far-right on Capitol Hill gets a slap on the wrist: According to the Seattle Times , “In a May 5 interview with the office of police accountability, the lieutenant reportedly denied making those statements until after he was shown the footage.” Memory is such a fickle thing. The Seattle Police Department faced a lot of backlash for beating the shit out of local community members protesting a Christian Supremacist rally in their backyard, and new police leaders don’t seem interested in doing much about it.

Not all of Indiana’s ACLU is down with Nikkita Oliver’s anti-Zionism: The Indianapolis Star reports some senior attorneys are leaving as the former left-wing Seattle City Council candidate takes over as executive director. What’s the issue? Nikkita comes from the activist world, not the legal and policy nerd world, and actually believing in equality is always controversial in the progressive nonprofit world. “Oliver’s social media posts regarding the Israeli-Palestinian conflict have also generated controversy inside the organization” and “Some staffers felt the repeated critical and broad references to Zionism were problematic.”

Farmworkers take their fight to Washington Supreme Court: The justices heard arguments last Thursday in the case of a Sunnyside mushroom farm in the middle of a long union battle, the Washington Observer reports . Farm owners wanted workers to accept reduced pay and sign away their rights to sue to keep their jobs—so you can understand why the workers are pissed. This can happen because farmworkers are denied equal rights to collectively bargain under federal law, and attempts in Washington state to give them those eights have been killed by corporate agricultural lobbying Democrats in Olympia.

Not all doctors wear stethoscopes: The big ass novelty check is one of America’s proudest inventions. Abro Ahmed of Minnesota got one from Superman after saving a runaway school bus full of kids after the bus driver suffered a medical emergency. He was able to do this by using the zen discipline he learned from Seattle-based doctor-sex television show Grey’s Anatomy : “[The show teaches] you about what to do in situations that you never could see yourself in,” Ahmed told ABC News . “So it’s just something like, you know, some tips and tricks that you could use for the rest of your life.”

Union journalists at second largest Washington paper want their editor out: Remember how the Spokesman-Review recently got their longtime scumbag Disney adult editor suspended after one inappropriate decision too many? Well, the paper’s owners want to keep him on but in a different role as the paper transitions into a nonprofit, and the union is throwing down the gauntlet, RANGE reports . The editor didn’t respond to a request for comment because he “is out on a Disney boat cruise through the end of this week,” according to the union.

The Pacific Northwest is getting a new experimental missile range: Montana is already home to more nuclear missiles than just about anywhere else in the world (Western Washington is a close competitor), but the prairie might see a lot more fire soon. Republicans are planning a new bombing range in the state for hypersonic missiles, those things the Iranians, Yemenis, and Russians are using to outshoot us and our useless, expensive fighter jets, the Billings Gazette reports . The tribes will likely not be happy about this. The US Army previously built its largest domestic base of the 19th century in Montana to keep them down.

Hitler News: Someone burned down Hitler’s ski chalet: It’s kind of wild that the “Eagle’s Nest” in Bavaria was still around after all these years, but an enterprising arsonist appears to have tidied up this particular historical anomaly, the AP reports . The chalet is in Bertchesgaden, and part of a complex of Bavarian mountain bungalows built for the Nazi Party elite. They’re the same bungalows our proud lads get drunk and loot at the end of Band of Brothers .

Canadians asked CIA for approval to release secret report on resettled Nazi war criminals: After decades of coverups, the report was finally released earlier this month after a court order required it. The court order was the result of the Canadian Parliament giving a standing ovation to a veteran of the Nazi Party’s Waffen-SS praetorian guard, infuriating Jewish groups, who sued. The details of the report were so damning—they prove the CIA used Canada as a dumping ground for perpetrators of the Holocaust who had outlived their usefulness as anti-commiunist intelligence agents—that the Canadian government warned the CIA that the secret was about to come out. There’s still redacted information in the report, the Maple reports .

Mac loved the rabbit, that’s just the point! Last week, I watched charming little comedy Local Hero (1983), which is a sort of reverse- Avatar film about a brave oil company operative trying to save a remote Scottish town from itself by demolishing the place and replacing it with a North Sea oil refinery. Everyone in town is actually on board with this for once, but whimsy happens. Anyway, I can’t get the soundtrack by Mark Knopfler of Dire Straits out of my head.

articles.title: Earwax is both slippery and sticky – this weird combo might lead to safer insect repellents
articles.author:
<name>David Hu, Professor of Mechanical Engineering and Biology, Adjunct Professor of Physics, Georgia Institute of Technology</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/david-hu-204122"/>
paras: Here’s a bit of a riddle for you: What has the consistency of both toothpaste and dough, can absorb twice its weight in water and still remain sticky, was used by medieval artists as a binder in paint and has been hypothesized by physicians to repel insects?

The medical term for earwax is cerumen, based on keros, the Greek word for beeswax. People have been pondering earwax since ancient times. Ancient hygiene kits including picks and spoons to remove earwax have been found in archaeological sites worldwide .

Even today, it remains a perpetual question: to remove or not to remove your earwax? The answer: Don’t do it . The general medical belief is that ears are self-cleaning , and earwax brings benefits such as lubricating the ear canal, fighting infection and acting like a sticky net to trap debris before it reaches the eardrum. By poking in there you can accidentally make matters worse, pushing wax deeper or scratching your delicate ear canal.

Cerumen impaction – or blocked earwax – affects about a fifth of the American population , leading to 12 million patient visits per year. Blockages are worsened by daily activities such as wearing earbuds or hearing aids.

Another common problem with ears is wedged debris. For children, much of this is self-inflicted, in the form of items such as Legos or erasers. But for many adults who have something stuck in their ear, the debris is insects, such as ants, beetles, flies or cockroaches.

While rare for the average person, insects in the ear occurred with such frequency over the years that physicians began to wonder whether earwax evolved as a natural barrier for insects. But how would such a barrier work?

To answer this question, my Ph.D. student David Ancalle led experiments with earwax and insects. We teamed up with Yuhang Hu and her student Donjing He , experts in the behavior of soft solids such as hydrogels. As mechanical engineers, we wanted to focus on the physics rather than the chemistry of earwax.
Our research , published in the journal Soft Matter, shows that earwax can, in fact, stop insects without the use of dangerous chemicals.
To do experiments, we needed voluminous amounts of earwax.

Initially we obtained earwax from deceased mammals such as pigs, sheep and rabbits. Eventually we turned to our friends and family. A person has only a grain of rice’s worth of earwax in each ear. Due to a mutation in a single gene , East Asians have dry, flaky earwax, while people of African or European descent have wet, squishy earwax .

To simulate an ant climbing into an ear canal, we used a glass beaker with its rim coated in earwax. Ants, like many insects, are climbing specialists, capable of traveling across many kinds of surfaces. To climb rough surfaces, ants have spikes on their feet , like mountain climbers do, that helps them grasp onto ridges and cracks. For smooth surfaces, ants unfurl wet suction cups , which can support 60 times their body weight on smooth glass.
Watching ants trying to climb earwax showed us how strange a substance it really is. Rough earwax slowed them down, but with their claws they made progress.
But as soon as ants tried to climb smooth earwax, they fell immediately.
From these experiments, we concluded that earwax had anti-stick properties when in contact with the insects’ feet.

We next conducted experiments with ants crawling through an earwax-coated tunnel, more similar in size to a human ear canal. As the ants attempted to travel through the tunnel, earwax stuck to them. Once coated, they groomed furiously, unwilling to walk until they had removed as much as possible. Even after several minutes of effort, the ants still had earwax sticking to hard-to-reach places.

So, earwax is a paradoxical material: It is simultaneously slippery, thanks to the lipids it contains, but also sticky. Similar to many materials – including ketchup, paint and shampoo – it thins out when it is physically deformed, what physicists call shear-thinning.

The dual qualities of earwax have to do with its unique composition. Earwax is made up of flakes of skin cells held together with a binder. This blend forms a kind of sponge with microscopic holes. When a body overproduces earwax, it heaps up in boulders that ants can easily climb over.

When the substance is smooth, however, ants rely on their wet suction cups. The holes in the earwax absorb the drops produced by the ants, preventing them from attaching. Absorbency makes earwax fundamentally different from commonly used forms of pest control.

In your local store, you will find sticky surfaces such as fly paper or chemicals that kill the insects. Some researchers look to nature to find bio-friendly alternatives to using chemicals; for example, plants have properties that prevent insects from climbing .
From this study, we learned that the ear is also a model for insect repellency. Earwax is made of natural materials but has a structure that prevents ants from sticking to it.

The porosity of earwax also gives it unique properties. We showed it can absorb twice its weight in water yet still cling to the walls of the ear. This water-absorbing ability may help prevent water from accumulating on the delicate eardrum and fend off infections such as swimmer’s ear .
Scientists don’t yet understand the complex relationship between earwax, water and bacteria. Some studies show that earwax kills bacteria , but other studies find that earwax harbors bacteria .

Our experiments showed that earwax is most challenging to insects when similar to the thin layer of earwax maintained by a healthy human body. Wax would accumulate more in human ears if not for two self-cleaning mechanisms. The skin in the ear canal grows outward like a conveyor belt. Over 8-10 weeks, this process – called epithelial migration – pushes the oldest earwax out of the ear.

Simultaneously, earwax dries over time, transforming from a gooey state to a brittle one that readily cracks. Every time you talk or chew , your ear canal deforms , and physicians found that this movement helps to dislodge the drier, older earwax.

As a test of our concept, a member of our team, chemical engineer Rafeen Rahaman, designed an artificial earwax based on the physical structure rather than the chemistry of the earwax. Ants struggled when they touched it, just like when they interacted with natural earwax.

The cost of harvesting natural earwax and our recipe for artificial earwax are not cheap. We don’t foresee our methods replacing insect repellents produced at large scale. But perhaps the concept might inspire new ways to prevent earwax from coating our earbuds or lead to the manufacture of insect control methods using safe formulations.

articles.title: School librarians are vanishing from Michigan schools just when they are needed most
articles.author:
<name>Shannon Oltmann, Associate Dean of Information Sciences, Wayne State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/shannon-oltmann-2762896"/>
paras: Fewer than 10% of Michigan public schools report having a school library staffed with a trained school librarian.

Although Michigan strongly recommends that schools employ certified librarians , the state does not require them. In the 2023–24 school year, the state ranked 46th in the student-to-librarian ratio , with one school librarian for every 2,760 students.

The lack of school librarians impacts students across Michigan, but particularly in low-income communities like Detroit and Flint and more isolated ones like Alcona County in the northern Lower Peninsula and Ontonagon in the Upper Peninsula, exacerbating disparities in resources for young people.

We are scholars in library and information sciences from Wayne State University , studying information access and ethics and equity in education and school libraries . Currently, we are conducting a statewide campaign to contact every school in Michigan and learn about their libraries, staffing, book collections, technology resources and more.

Michigan’s 2025–26 School Aid budget funded our statewide survey to measure the school librarian shortage and guide efforts to address it. Our work, and the work of many others, reveals how school librarians help students become strong readers and informed citizens.

A missing librarian is harder to see than an empty bookshelf. A room full of books can look like a school library. But if students cannot borrow those books, teachers have no librarian to plan lessons with, and no one leads author visits or digital citizenship lessons, the space offers only a fraction of what a school library can provide.

School librarians bring those services to life. Also called school library media specialists, they hold a teaching certificate and complete advanced education . They connect students with books they want to read and work with teachers to build richer lessons, using library resources to extend learning beyond the textbook.

Their impact stretches far beyond standardized test scores, though studies link strong library programs with higher student achievement and improved student literacy , especially for struggling readers . They can instill a love of reading and teach technological skills , which is critical in the age of artificial intelligence.

At our Michigan School Census symposium held in 2026, Michigan school librarians and a principal described what that work looks like. Brian Peck, a teacher librarian at Detroit’s UPrep Academy, helped students research and build a library where none had existed. He reported that 334 students voluntarily visited and checked out books during the previous school year.

At West Ottawa, librarian Julia Reynolds described replacing crowded shelves with displays that let children see book covers. Circulation quadrupled, she reported. A principal on the panel explained how district support helped schools make library visits a priority from the first week of school.
Access to information is only a start. Students also need help making sense of what reaches them through searches, social media and AI.
AI can create convincing fake videos of students doing or saying things they never did, harming their reputations and undermining trust in what people see online.

Less visible forces shape students’ information worlds, too. Algorithms and online platforms often dictate which search results and suggested videos appear first. Students need to understand that the first result is not necessarily the most credible or trustworthy source. AI is becoming so prominent that even elementary school students are learning about it.
Information literacy means knowing how to find, judge and use information. School librarians turn those skills into practice.
For a history assignment, a librarian might help students compare a newspaper account with a firsthand record. Who produced each source? What might explain their different accounts?
The same habits apply to AI. Students can trace a claim to its source, check whether the source exists and compare what it says with the generated answer. A confident response still needs evidence.

Guided by certified school librarians, students can build upon these foundations and learn to effectively find, evaluate and use information, including news articles about a historic event for a social studies assignment or to analyze current social media trends. Students can also judge the accuracy, recency and relevance of information. They learn to apply information in decision-making, writing and other forms of communication.
Knowing whether information is trustworthy is an important skill. Deciding what to do with it is another.
Digital citizenship includes deciding whether to post someone’s photo, seeking their permission before doing so, and choosing not to share a fake video.
Recent research emphasizes that digital citizenship prepares students to be empowered online and act ethically, safely and legally in digital environments.
Our work also starts with the knowledge young people bring to school.

Project Restoring Urban School Libraries helped classroom teachers earn the additional endorsement needed to become school librarians. The program combined mentoring with coursework that drew on students’ cultures, including using hip-hop to explore how young people find, create and share information.
Students start by examining the media they already use. A lesson might ask them to trace a sample, credit its creator and discuss what changes when someone else’s work reaches a new audience.

Principal preparation programs can help school leaders understand what school librarians contribute beyond book checkout. But principals and school librarians often train in separate academic units: colleges of education and schools of library and information science. Without shared coursework or joint projects, principals may complete their training without learning how to work with a school librarian.

In our “Closing the Literacy Gap” symposium, we brought school librarians and administrators together on a panel to show what their partnerships make possible. West Ottawa Principal Audra Bolhuis joined school librarian Julia Reynolds and compared a librarian to “ an instructional coach .” She described someone teachers can turn to for resources and help with classroom projects, extending the librarian’s role beyond students’ scheduled library visits.
School library jobs remain vulnerable to budget cuts , and the number of school librarians across the state has been decreasing since 2010.

To understand what schools provide and where support is missing, we launched the state-funded Michigan School Census in September 2026. By Oct. 21, 1,054 schools – about one-third of those invited – had completed it. Our public response map tracks participation across districts.

Schools without libraries or librarians are essential to painting the full picture: Their staff can explain how students get books and research help when those services are absent. The findings will guide recommendations for staffing, resources and funding.
Counting what schools have is the first step toward deciding what every Michigan student should be able to count on.
Read more of our stories about Detroit and Michigan .

The funding was routed through the Michigan Department of Education, to Wayne State University, then to my School. I do not benefit directly from funding (i.e., no income). Second, I am a recipient of a current National Leadership Grant from the Institute of Museum and Library Services, for $445,000. This grant funds research to study how public libraries respond to censorship.

articles.title: We studied 1,584 data centers – and found the buildings full of machines are tied to modest local job growth
articles.author:
<name>Simon Buechler, Assistant Professor of Finance, Miami University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/simon-buechler-2769962"/>
paras: Data centers require enormous investments : land, buildings, computer equipment and power infrastructure. Yet, once they’re up and running, they tend to employ no more than a few dozen people in occupations such as IT technicians, engineers and security guards. With billions of dollars flowing into new data centers across the United States, communities are asking what they will get in return .

Skepticism about the local benefits of data centers is contributing to growing opposition to their construction , from Ohio to Texas . That pushback contributed to delays or cancellations of US$156 billion in proposed data center projects in 2025 alone.

We are professors who study real estate and urban economics , including how large place-based investments shape local economies. So we set out to answer a question at the center of these fights: Do data centers actually create jobs where they are built?

To find out, we teamed up with four colleagues to study what happens to local employment after data centers open. We found that new data centers that opened from 2000-2023 created 1,000 to 1,300 jobs in the counties where they are located, on average. But those jobs, which are for work performed outside data centers rather than inside them, take a few years to appear. They are mostly in industries that support data centers, not in restaurants or shops.
Data centers can create jobs in at least three ways beyond employing people who work inside them.
First, they can increase demand for local suppliers, from security companies that protect the facilities to electrical contractors that maintain their equipment.
Second, data center employees and workers at these suppliers may spend more money locally, supporting restaurants, stores and other local services.

Third, companies already operating data centers may expand their facilities, while other operators may decide to build nearby. Once a location has the electricity, fiber connections and other infrastructure needed to operate a data center, further investment may become easier.

We assembled detailed information on 1,584 U.S. data centers that opened between 2000 and 2023. For each facility, we recorded its location, opening date and power capacity, which is a standard way to compare facilities of different sizes. We then matched these records with federal data on employment, wages and the number of businesses in each county.

Isolating the effect of data centers isn’t straightforward. Operators don’t choose locations randomly. They look for reliable electricity, fiber connections, available land and friendly local regulations. Those places may already be growing, so new jobs might have appeared even without a data center.

To account for this, we tracked employment in counties that received data centers – such as Loudoun County in Virginia, Berkeley County in South Carolina, Morrow County in Oregon, and others – before and after the operation of the facility began. We then compared those trends with similar counties that did not receive data centers. We also looked at whether larger facilities brought bigger job gains.

During the first two years after a county’s first data center opened, we found little change in employment outside construction. After that, jobs begin to grow. Three to five years after a center opened, we found that these counties had roughly 1,000 to 1,300 additional nonconstruction jobs than comparable counties without data centers.
Bigger investments brought bigger employment gains. Five years after new data center capacity is installed, each additional megawatt is associated with about 7.4 more nonconstruction local jobs.

Part of that gain, however, reflects further expansion. Each megawatt installed is associated with another 1.7 megawatts of capacity over the following years. Once that later growth is counted, our estimates work out to about 2.7 nonconstruction jobs per megawatt of eventual data center capacity. A large 100-megawatt facility, for example, would be correlated with roughly 275 additional local jobs outside the data center itself.
The types of jobs created help explain what is happening.

Employment gains are concentrated in transportation and warehousing, professional and technical services and real estate. These industries may serve or benefit directly from data centers or from the investment and infrastructure they bring.
By contrast, we found little evidence of job growth in restaurants, stores and other local services.

We also found that more data center investment tends to follow in the same county. Most often, the companies already operating in a county expand their facilities. Other companies generally don’t move into that same area to build new data centers.

Our study has limits. It covers data centers that opened through 2023, before the current wave of massive facilities were built to power AI. Larger data centers do not necessarily create proportionally more jobs, so our findings may not apply to today’s biggest projects.

We also looked only at job gains and did not explore whether data centers are worth their cost to local communities. These facilities consume large amounts of electricity and water, can generate noise and may receive substantial tax breaks from local and state governments. We did not address any of those concerns.

Our findings do show that data centers can create jobs beyond the small number of people working inside their walls. But that does not mean every one of them is a good deal for their local community. And whether those additional jobs justify the costs remains an open question.

articles.title: Leave home with a plan: What to pack in your medical kit and when to seek care for symptoms abroad
articles.author:
<name>Andrés Henao, Professor of Medicine and Infectious Disease, University of Colorado Anschutz</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/andres-henao-2702942"/>
paras: When people prepare to see a doctor before an international trip, vaccines usually dominate the conversation.

And while vaccines are important, many of the health problems most likely to derail a trip cannot be prevented with a vaccine: Diarrhea, respiratory infections, motion sickness and flare-ups of existing medical conditions are all common – and none of them can be headed off with a shot.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that between 43% and 79% of travelers to low- and middle-income countries become ill during or after their trip, although most of those illnesses are mild.
As an infectious diseases physician who specializes in travel and tropical medicine, I counsel many patients before they leave the country and care for them when they come home sick.

A good pretravel visit to the doctor should end with more than a list of shots. You should know which illnesses you could encounter on your itinerary, which symptoms you can reasonably handle yourself, which medicines to carry and how to use them, and which warning signs mean it is time to find a doctor.

Infectious disease risks abroad are constantly shifting. A good healthcare provider who specializes in travel and geographic medicine keeps up with these developments so that the advice you get reflects what is happening now, not last year.
Since early 2025, South America has seen new yellow fever outbreaks that redrew long-standing risk maps and an unusual hantavirus cluster that spread from person to person aboard a cruise ship .

Cases of dengue fever worldwide roughly doubled in a single year , and another tropical disease – chikungunya – also flared in new places, including the largest outbreak ever recorded in China . Fiji declared a fast-growing HIV outbreak . And common respiratory viruses, from influenza to COVID-19, continue to circulate all over the world.

In my own clinical research with colleagues, we have seen travelers who returned to the U.S. with serious – and occasionally fatal – infections, such as malaria and hepatitis , often after dangerous delays in recognizing what was wrong.
Travel health advice is not one-size-fits-all. A week at a Caribbean resort, a safari in East Africa and a month trekking in Nepal carry very different risks.

Even the likely cause of a fever changes with the destination. Dengue is a leading concern after travel in much of Latin America and Asia, while malaria is especially important in parts of sub-Saharan Africa, and typhoid and paratyphoid fever loom largest in South Asia.
What you do matters, too – freshwater swimming, visiting caves, animal contact, hiking and staying in remote areas each add their own hazards .

So bring your actual itinerary to the appointment. Tell your doctor not just which countries you’ll visit, but whether you’ll be in cities or the countryside, what you plan to do, how high you’ll go, how long you’ll stay and how easily you could reach a reliable hospital.

For minor illnesses, you can plan to treat yourself. Travelers’ diarrhea is the best example of such an illness. Depending on the destination and season, it affects an estimated 10% to 40% of travelers during the first two weeks of a trip. Most cases clear up on their own within a few days, but having a plan makes a real difference.

Ask your doctor what to do if diarrhea develops. Oral rehydration salts help replace fluids when losses are heavy. Loperamide , an over-the-counter antidiarrheal, can reduce how often and how urgently you need a bathroom, but it should not be used on its own when diarrhea comes with a fever or blood in the stool. Depending on your destination and medical history, your doctor may also give you an antibiotic to carry and use only for moderate or severe diarrhea.

When it comes to treatments you’ll be administering yourself, it’s as important to ask your doctor when to use each medicine as it is to have the drugs on hand. Antibiotics have side effects, can leave you carrying drug-resistant bacteria and contribute to antibiotic resistance worldwide – so they are best saved for the episodes that truly need them.

The same logic applies to other predictable problems. Someone prone to seasickness on a planned boat trip might discuss meclizine or a scopolamine patch . A traveler flying straight into a high-altitude city such as Cusco, Peru, or La Paz, Bolivia, might discuss acetazolamide, a prescription medicine that helps the body acclimatize and roughly halves the risk of altitude sickness during rapid ascents.

A basic travel health kit keeps a small problem from becoming a big one. The contents depend on the traveler and the trip, but useful items include pain and fever medicine, bandages, antiseptic, oral rehydration salts , loperamide , antihistamine and anything prescribed specifically for the trip.

People with chronic conditions should pack enough of their regular medications for the entire trip, plus extra in case of delays. Keep medicines in their original labeled containers, carry them in your hand luggage rather than checked bags, and consider bringing a copy of your prescriptions written with the drugs’ generic names.

Replacing a medication abroad can be harder than you expect. Drugs may have different names, formulations or availability in other countries, and counterfeit or low-quality medicines remain a real problem in some places. Some medications that are routine in the U.S. are restricted or banned elsewhere. Insulin, injectable drugs, controlled substances and anything that needs refrigeration will require extra planning.

Travel medicine is full of remedies with better reputations than evidence. Ginger is often recommended for motion sickness, but studies have produced mixed results . Acupressure wristbands for motion sickness do not outperform placebos . And despite their popularity, probiotics are not recommended for preventing travelers’ diarrhea , as their efficacy is still unknown.

Coca leaves and coca tea are widely used for altitude symptoms in the Andes, but there is no strong evidence that they prevent altitude illness – and the same is true of garlic, ginkgo and vitamin E. “ Natural” does not mean effective , or even harmless, particularly when a supplement interacts with a prescription drug .
Perhaps the most important part of any plan is recognizing when self-care is no longer appropriate.

Seek medical attention for severe dehydration, persistent vomiting, difficulty breathing, confusion, severe abdominal pain or an illness that is rapidly getting worse. Bloody diarrhea or diarrhea with a significant fever calls for medical care rather than simply taking an antidiarrheal and carrying on with your trip.

At high altitudes, shortness of breath while resting, confusion, or difficulty walking a straight line are warning signs. Severe altitude illness is treated by descending and getting medical care – another cup of coca tea is not an adequate substitute.

Fever after travel to an area where malaria is common deserves special attention. Malaria can turn deadly within hours, so get evaluated promptly and make sure the clinician knows where you have been. Some travel-related infections surface weeks or even months after you get home , which is why your travel history stays relevant long after your suitcase is unpacked.

I encourage travelers to make a medical contingency plan. Ask yourself: If my flight home were canceled and I had to stay abroad another week, would I have enough medication? If I developed diarrhea tomorrow, would I know what to take? If I spiked a fever, would I know when and where to seek care?
International travel will never be risk-free. But preparing for the problems most likely to happen can keep a manageable illness from becoming a medical emergency.

articles.title: How should AI be regulated? Follow the harm
articles.author:
<name>Sylvia Lu, Assistant Professor of Law, American University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/sylvia-lu-2222047"/>
paras: As artificial intelligence technologies grow ever more powerful, so do the risks they pose and with them the urgency of regulating AI.

In July 2026, OpenAI’s advanced models hacked into AI company Hugging Face’s systems during internal cybersecurity evaluations by communicating through unauthorized channels and working around safeguards developers had imposed on the models. In January 2026, Google and Character.ai, which makes a role-playing AI chatbot, agreed to settle a wrongful death lawsuit brought by Megan Garcia. Her 14-year-old son, who used the chatbot heavily, died by suicide.
As these and other cases show, AI harms can emerge across different technologies, organizations and contexts. As a legal scholar focused on AI and digital harms , I study how to regulate AI.

Policymakers and industry commentators have tended to frame regulation as a trade-off between the risks of AI and the risks of regulating AI. In its 2025 AI Action Plan , the Trump administration called for removing “red tape and onerous regulation,” which it said hinders economic growth. The administration has also sought to limit conflicting state AI laws.

In contrast to the broad concerns about the costs of AI regulation, AI harms have largely been addressed through rules specific to particular technologies. The federal Take It Down Act, signed in 2025, for example, addresses nonconsensual intimate imagery , including AI-generated deepfakes, as do various state laws . These approaches are crucial, but they don’t solve the problem by themselves.

The emerging patchwork of rules has yet to establish a regulatory architecture that connects protected interests, institutional obligations and individual rights across AI technologies. Protected interests are rights recognized by the law, such as property ownership and personal privacy. A harm-centered approach would begin with those interests and use them to shape legal obligations that span relevant systems, organizations and people.
A harm-centered approach starts by identifying the fundamental interests that AI systems can threaten. These overlapping interests include:
These examples are not exhaustive. Other interests may also be at stake as AI technologies evolve.

The same interest can be threatened by different technologies and different entities. A teenager’s safety can be harmed by the engagement mechanisms of a social media platform or by an AI companion designed to sustain an emotional relationship.

Designing regulations based on a concept of harm allows laws and principles to follow problems as the technology changes. And it helps determine obligations imposed on developers, deployers and other stakeholders involved in AI.

For instance, AI developers could be required to conduct harm assessments throughout the development of AI systems, identifying reasonably foreseeable harms, documenting how they tested for them and explaining what mitigation measures they took. Companies or government agencies that deploy AI systems could also have duties to monitor harms after deployment. Serious or recurring harms could trigger obligations to report them to relevant regulators, affected individuals or the public, depending on the nature and severity of the harm.

A harm-centered framework could also recognize corresponding rights for people affected by AI systems, including rights to notice and opportunities to seek redress where appropriate. These rights would arise from the same protected interests that justify obligations on companies.

The point is to build a regulatory architecture on the detection and reduction of harm across AI applications, developers and users. What matters most is whether and how AI-enabled design or operation contribute to harm.
This mindset is followed in other areas of law.

Environmental law, for instance, has long regulated industries by focusing on their environmental effects rather than on technology alone. It requires regulated companies to monitor emissions and discharges, maintain records and report specified releases to regulators . Some reporting requirements also make information available to the public. Environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act requires federal agencies to assess environmental effects and provides opportunities for public participation.
AI governance could draw on this logic, determining who is responsible for assessment, monitoring, disclosure and mitigation based on types of harm.

A harm-based focus would not eliminate technology-specific rules. Some technologies create distinctive risks that justify targeted rules, such as disclosure requirements for AI-generated deepfakes or safeguards for AI systems used in high-stakes decisions. And focusing on harm does not mean regulating every conceivable risk of harm.

But I believe that harm should become the organizing principle of AI regulation. New AI systems will bring harms policymakers have not yet anticipated. The challenge is to build a framework for the harms we know, as well as the harms we do not yet know.

articles.title: Viruses obey the laws of physics – studying how can help researchers understand why they infect people differently and lead to better treatments
articles.author:
<name>Tori Russell, Ph.D. Candidate in Biomedical and Chemical Engineering, Rochester Institute of Technology</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/tori-russell-2759278"/>
paras: The beauty of physics at the cellular scale is part of what draws biomedical engineers and biologists like us to the field of mechanobiology : the study of how physical forces influence biology.

Physics holds relevance everywhere . You can see physics at work on how the cells lining your veins and arteries feel the flow of your blood, the cells of your spinal discs carry the weight of the vertebrae surrounding them, and the cells of your lung cyclically stretch with every breath.

If each and every building block of the body experiences some combination of these physical forces, then the viruses that infect them must contend with a variation of those forces, too. How viruses interact with these forces affects how well they can infect cells and cause severe illness.
When microscopic virus particles enter the body, they rely upon the mechanical machinery of the cells they infect to continue their life cycle.

Many viruses will first latch onto receptors on the cell’s surface. Movement of the cell’s membrane – driven by its internal cytoskeleton – will bend and wrap around the invading particle, pinching off a tiny bubble that carries it inside. In this process of endocytosis , the cell swallows the virus.

Once inside, the virus is shuttled along the cell’s internal scaffolding. It releases its genetic material and hijacks the cell’s machinery to make copies of itself. New virus particles will then exit the cell to infect its neighbors.

Each of these steps is physical at its core. The tautness of a cell’s membrane could make it easier or harder to wrap around a virus. The cytoskeleton that transports these virus particles is the same lining that cells use to sense and push against their surroundings . What’s more, the stiffness of a cell’s environment will shape how the cell spreads and organizes itself , which may change how susceptible it is to an invader.

A healthy individual often can quickly recover from an infection. However, for someone with a preexisting condition such as pulmonary fibrosis – where the tissue of the lungs has stiffened and can no longer stretch to full capacity – a viral infection may make their condition worse.
This mechanical predisposition of tissues to infection is one reason health professionals urge the public when sick to avoid the elderly and immunocompromised.

Our laboratory looks into the mechanobiology of different types of tissues to understand how the physical forces people endure in daily life can worsen disease. Repetitive lifting and loading can wear down the discs of the spine , for example, and mechanical ventilators can overstretch and injure lungs .

But growing cells in a plastic petri dish – the standard method in most virology labs – shows only part of the story. Tissue culture plastic is significantly stiffer than living tissues , closer to a countertop than a lung. Cells notice the difference during experiments; the stiffness of their surroundings can change both how they behave and how they respond to an infection.

To bring the mechanics of the human body into the lab, we grow lung cells on thin layers of a flexible, silicone-based polymer called PDMS that we fine-tuned to match the softness of actual lung tissue. These sheets sit in small chambers that will cyclically stretch and relax on command from a computer that sets how far and how long they stretch. This allows us to mimic the physical movements of breathing.
We can use a virus engineered to make infected cells glow red under a microscope to monitor how it spreads among cells. But how can we monitor how the mechanics of a cell change during infection?

Our team follows the activity of two important proteins, YAP and TAZ , that act as the cell’s force sensors. When a tissue experiences stiffness or tension, these sensors will move into the nucleus and turn on genes tied to growth and repair. When those forces are lacking, as is generally the case in softer tissue, YAP and TAZ remain inactive and stay put outside of the nucleus.

Some viruses are known to tap into this same signaling pathway , so examining YAP and TAZ may offer a window into whether mechanical forces and infection influence one another. Using the gene-editing tool CRISPR , we can attach a fluorescent tag onto YAP or TAZ and watch their activation in real time under a microscope as they react not only to mechanical forces but potentially to infection as well.

With this platform, we can better answer questions such as whether lung cells will respond to infection differently under different forces or whether these forces will change how well viruses infect. Thus far, our early findings suggest that the stiffness of a cell’s environment affects how heavily cells become infected: Lung cells grown on stiffer, fibrosis-like surfaces appear to become more heavily infected.

Understanding the mechanics of viral infection is of particular interest to researchers and clinicians, given the persistent prevalence of respiratory infections worldwide. The common cold, COVID-19 and the flu represent merely a drop in the viral infection bucket: More than 200 species of virus are known to infect humans.

Mechanobiology may be just as important to the cycle of infection as its biochemical or immunological aspects. Under a microscope, the differences are clear between a stiff, overworked lung and a soft, healthy lung, and viruses may navigate these environments in adaptive ways.

As scientists map these mechanical signals, new possibilities for preventing and treating infection are opening up. Among them are therapies that could reduce the physical strain on tissues or even biomarkers that could tell patients whether they are susceptible to tissue stiffening or certain infection paths and the possible damage they may cause.
The human body is just as mechanical as it is chemical, and so, too, are the infections it encounters.

articles.title: Most Puget Sound Cities Aren't Keeping Up With Housing Growth Targets
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: A small number of cities across central Puget Sound are pulling along the entire region when it comes to keeping pace with long-term housing growth targets, according to new data released by the Puget Sound Regional Council (PSRC). Of the 40 cities across King, Pierce, Snohomish and Kitsap Counties that are expected to accommodate the largest share of regional housing growth through 2044, just 14 are on track and many are significantly behind.

The data provides a snapshot of uneven urban growth, more than a half-decade after a pivot in the four-county region's housing growth strategy toward transit investments that were either already in place or coming online. Though that strategy is clearly bearing some fruit, with cities like Shoreline, Redmond, and Mountlake Terrace easily dispatching with their targets, these numbers also point to the need for potential reforms around land use and building regulations elsewhere – some of which are already in motion.

"The region is producing housing at pace to meet its targets, but this is largely led by just a handful of jurisdictions," Eric Clute, a planner in PSRC's data department, said last week while breaking down the data for local elected officials. "I think these jurisdictions can offer a blueprint to others looking to boost production and meet their housing targets."

The adopted growth targets on the books right now across the urban areas of all four counties plan for a total of approximately 620,000 new units of housing by 2044, with close to half of that in King County. As a whole, the region has been outpacing that target, adding around 183,000 units since 2019 or 2020 – the start year varies by county, with the clock starting for King County in 2019, compared to 2020 for the other three counties.

That growth rate is around 16,000 more units than was needed to keep pace. But without growth in Seattle significantly outpacing its growth target – 70,000 units were built compared to a prorated growth target of just over 31,000 – the region as a whole would not be ahead of the overall target. Falling short will mean that Washington will likely fail to add the 1.1 million overall homes needed over the next two decades to tread water on housing affordability, according to the state's Commerce Department.

PSRC's Vision 2050 growth strategy lays out different tiers of jurisdictions expected to shoulder decreasing shares of regional housing growth. At the top are the metro cities, including Seattle, Tacoma, Bellevue, Everett, and Bremerton. These cities have the biggest growth targets, though a smaller overall target for Kitsap County means some cities across the Sound are aiming for more housing than Bremerton.

Out of those five, only Seattle outpaced its growth target, with Everett lagging the most. Snohomish County's largest city logged just over 2,000 new homes compared to an overall target of 36,500 by 2044. Bellevue did better , seeing more than 5,000 units built against a similar target. Tacoma saw more than 7,000 new units, but has an even more ambitious growth target of 43,000.

Just below those five big kahunas are the "core cities," mid-sized jurisdictions that are also expected to carry a significant amount of regional growth. Just four out of 15 of those cities – Redmond, Kirkland, Issaquah and Kent – are meeting or exceeding their targets. Renton, Auburn and Federal are falling the furthest short, while Lynnwood and Bothell are doing better.

Outside of metro and core cities, another set of cities known as "high capacity transit (HCT) communities" are also planning for a fairly significant share of growth. HCT communities feature some type of current or future transit investments, from a Sounder commuter or Link light rail station to a planned bus rapid transit line.

Nine of those 20 cities are on track, with Shoreline leading the pack. Woodinville, Mountlake Terrace, and Port Orchard are other standouts here, with Edmonds falling significantly short of expectations. DuPont, which had been set to see an extension of Sound Transit's S Line until an agency board vote earlier this year through a construction timeline into limbo , saw essentially no housing growth at all.

The good news here is that required updates to local growth plans made by the end of 2024, along with required zoning adjustments to allow more types of housing in lower density neighborhoods the following year, are just starting to bear fruit. In the metro cities specifically, many of those adjustments were bold ones, including the Home in Tacoma rezones and Bellevue's land use code reforms that targeted areas ripe for redevelopment, like Wilburton .

"We have all made recent updates to Comprehensive Plans that made significant changes to spur housing production," Clute said. "These changes are likely not yet showing up in the data. Those changes were done just a couple years ago, or a year ago, and development takes several years to happen."

And then there are the cities and towns that are not expected to shoulder as much growth, places like North Bend, Gig Harbor, and Lake Stevens. Growth in those places, on the whole, has been significantly outpacing growth targets, a fact that stands in stark contrast with the bigger cities that are lagging behind.

What about urban unincorporated areas? Areas outside cities and towns but still inside the urban growth area (UGA) saw significant growth in Pierce County, and less growth in Snohomish and Kitsap Counties. King County's modest urban unincorporated growth target is right on pace.

Slower-than-expected growth in unincorporated Kitsap County is likely good news for urbanists, who have argued that the growth plans for those areas set up suburban sprawl . On the other hand, unincorporated Snohomish County includes areas set to see light rail expansion, including the vicinity of the Ash Way and Mariner Park and Ride stations being built as part of Everett Link .

Ultimately, the numbers released last week could represent a new baseline, with housing production in Seattle slowing significantly and overhauled zoning across Puget Sound potentially setting the stage for increased growth elsewhere. If Seattle's steady homebuilding pace falters without other cities picking up the slack, the region could be in for more housing affordability woes.

While underlying land use regulations clearly aren't the only factor at play when it comes to regional growth, they do play a big role. And though the region as a whole may be slightly ahead of the curve, that's no reason for any city to sit on its laurels.

articles.title: How the Crosslake Connection Impacted Bus Ridership Patterns
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: On March 28, Sound Transit opened the much anticipated Crosslake Connection. This rail connection between Seattle and cities on the Eastside promised fast, frequent, and more reliable connectivity across Lake Washington. The Link 2 Line was designed to replace the hundreds of daily bus trips on I-90, freeing up service hours to improve local bus routes. Initially, however, the I-90 bus routes remained intact to offer extra capacity and redundancy during the World Cup. In the five months following the Crosslake Connection opening, passengers could either take the train or bus. Many chose to take the train. In August 2026, the 11 Link stations on the Eastside and Mercer Island accounted for 12,500 boardings each weekday.

This article will discuss the stop-level ridership data for select routes in east King County. To minimize the impact of seasonal changes in ridership, the analysis compares data from March-August 2025 with data from March-August 2026. The plots below show average weekday boardings and alightings at each stop, boardings are shown with positive bars, alightings are shown with negative bars. The different colors represent the number of passengers boarding/alighting during that time of day. The data for 2025 is shown as slightly faded. Click on each plot to open it in a new tab.
Sound Transit Express routes 550 and 554 provided all-day bus service across Lake Washington via I-90. Following the full 2 Line opening, many people switched from one of these routes to Link.

Overall ridership on Route 550 dropped 52% year-over-year. Boardings at the route’s busiest stop in 2025, Bellevue Transit Center, fell 57% as many passengers opted to take the 2 Line instead. Along Bellevue Way, the stop at 4th Street took the crown as the busiest stop with 278 weekday boardings (this stop had 366 weekday boardings in 2025). The other stops on Bellevue Way did not see significant changes in ridership. One stop that saw an increase in passenger boardings is South Bellevue station for Bellevue-bound trips. Passengers transferring from the 2 Line to Route 550 to access a stop on Bellevue Way doubled the boarding count to 50 per day. Route 550 stops near South Bellevue station and Mercer Island station. Seattle-bound boardings on Route 550 at those stops dropped by 78% and 74%, respectively.

Similar to Route 550, ridership on Route 554 fell where it overlaps with Link but remained constant elsewhere. Route 554’s stops in Issaquah had similar ridership to 2025. However, boardings at the Eastgate P&R (I-90 & 142nd Pl) fell 42%. This is likely due to more people choosing to use the nearby South Bellevue P&R and Link instead. On Mercer Island, the number of passengers boarding a Route 554 bus dropped 72% as many switched to the 2 Line. Route 554 was replaced by Route 556 in August. Route 556 provides more frequent service between Issaquah and Bellevue, via South Bellevue station and Bellevue Way.

State Route 520 is the only other connection between Seattle and the Eastside across Lake Washington. Some bus routes that use SR-520, such as Route 255, do not complete with the 2 Line and saw negligible changes in ridership patterns following the 2 Line opening. Other routes had significant changes as some passengers switched to the Link 2 Line.

While Route 545 takes a different route from Link across Lake Washington, it offers redundant service with the 2 Line between Redmond and downtown Seattle. Following the full 2 Line opening, ridership on the route fell 20%. At SR-520 & 40th St (near Redmond Technology station), inbound boardings fell 19%. Likewise, boardings at Redmond Transit Center dropped by 23%.

In downtown Seattle, Route 545 ridership has shifted north. Stops along Olive Way had a collective 2.5% increase in boardings, despite the closure of the peak-only stop at Boren Ave. Meanwhile, stops on 4th Ave had a collective 36% decrease in passenger boardings. This reflects passengers choosing to take the fastest trip. Route 545 is often faster than Link between the Denny Triangle and Redmond, while Link is usually faster between Redmond and CID or Pioneer Square. After all, Route 545 doesn’t save as much time as you think .

Compared to the 2 Line, Route 542 offers a shortcut between Redmond and the U District. A trip from the U District to downtown Redmond on Link takes 56 minutes vs just 32 minutes via Route 542. Ridership on this route has remained steady, with a 2.4% increase in boardings year-over-year. There were no significant changes to the route’s ridership patterns.

Route 271 also connected Seattle with the Eastside via SR-520. The long route had several noticeable changes in its ridership patterns following the opening of the Crosslake Connection. Trips between the U District and downtown Bellevue take 37 minutes on Link vs 24 minutes on Route 271. Despite the faster trip time on Route 271, the number of passengers boarding Seattle-bound trips at Bellevue Transit Center dropped 47%. This is likely from passengers who previously connected to another route in the U District and now have a more time-competitive option with Link (eg: trips from Bellevue to Capitol Hill).
Route 271 also had a 41% decrease in boardings at Eastgate Park & Ride. This is the same changed observed with Route 554 and is likely to due more people using the South Bellevue P&R instead.

The only new 2 Line station in Seattle, Judkins Park, impacted the ridership patterns of the five King County Metro routes that stop nearby: routes 7, 8, 9, 48, and 106. The intersection of an east-west Link station and five north-south bus routes is a key opportunity for many transfers. However, the data show that only 486 people are transferring between Link and one of the bus routes each weekday. This accounts for about ⅓ of boardings at Judkins Park station, a bit less than the projected 42% . The table below breaks down the bus boardings at Judkins Park station by route and direction.

The Crosslake Connection is already making its mark on travel patterns across Lake Washington. Many passengers switched from routes 271, 545, 550, and 554 to Link when it was the faster option. In Seattle, fewer people than expected are transferring between buses and the 2 Line at Judkins Park station.

The five month period of overlapping Link and bus service has come to a close and many bus routes were truncated in August . Seattle Transit Blog will share ridership data analysis from those changes in Spring 2027 (when the data are available).

In the meantime, explore detailed ridership data for most King County Metro, Sound Transit, and Community Transit routes at seattletransitridership.com . The dashboard has been updated to include stop-level data for all Metro and Metro operated Sound Transit routes from the Spring 2026 service change. The impact of the Federal Way Link Extension on bus routes in south King County will be discussed in an article tomorrow.

articles.title: ‘For Ayşenur’ — Central District mural will honor UW activist killed by Israeli forces
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: A new community mural honoring late University of Washington graduate and activist Ayşenur Ezgi Eygi is slated for installation on the grounds of Cherry Street Village in the Central District.
Permits with the city have been approved for a structure along the northern edge of the property at 720 25th Ave, near E Cherry.
Designed in partnership with Architects Without Borders – Seattle , the installation consists of three stacked panels of marine-grade plywood measuring roughly 12 feet wide by 8 feet tall.

The mural honors Eygi, a 26-year-old Seattle activist and UW psychology and Middle Eastern languages graduate who was killed in September 2024 by Israeli forces while demonstrating against settlement expansion in the West Bank. Prior to her death, Eygi had taken part in pro-Palestinian campus protests and negotiations at UW.

Designed by artist James Hesketh , the artwork depicts Eygi wearing a keffiyeh set against an olive tree, poppies, and tulips. More than 100 community members, friends, and family contributed to painting the panels paint-by-numbers style during a gathering at Cherry Street Village that marked what would have been her 28th birthday.
A segment representing Eygi was added to The Olympia-Rafah Solidarity Mural this fall (Image: @jameshesketh_ )

The Eygi mural project is being funded through donations and volunteer work and will add to the Central District’s collection of community murals including The People’s Wall at 19th and Spruce that received official city landmarks protections this summer.

Cherry Street Village is a social justice collective, community hub, and intentional living space co-directed by activist Samia El-Moslimany . Operating out of a property home to The Islamic School of Seattle into the 2010s, the village formed to host grassroots organizing, cultural events, mutual aid, and activist workshops. Today, it serves as a neighborhood gathering site for civil rights and solidarity efforts.

The new mural structure will stand one to two feet above the ground, supported by side posts and horizontal framing anchored into cast-in-place concrete piers. A small, cantilevered rooflet will sit atop the frame to shield the painted surface from Pacific Northwest weather.
Organizers have planned to unveil the permanent installation for neighborhood residents and passersby this fall.

articles.title: New superintendent, renewed closures: Capitol Hill’s Stevens Elementary proposed to merge into Montlake
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Families lined up against the closure in 2024

In a renewed push for campus consolidations amid declining districtwide enrollment, Seattle Public Schools has introduced a proposal to merge Capitol Hill’s Stevens Elementary into Montlake Elementary for the 2027–2028 school year,

“I don’t want students to spend one more year in a building where bookcases serve as walls, if we don’t have to,” Superintendent Ben Shuldiner wrote in a district newsletter this weekend as word of the renewed push spread.

“I don’t want students to spend one more year in a sixth-seventh-eighth grade split if we don’t have to. I don’t want teachers to be the only teacher in the grade if we don’t have to. I don’t want to accept large class sizes if we don’t have to. So, the conversation around school mergers begins.”

More accurately, the conversation re-starts. The announcement revives consolidation efforts that stalled two years ago. In late 2024, Seattle Public Schools backed away from a plan that would have shuttered up to 21 elementary campuses, including the Stevens campus along 19th Ave E at Galer just east of Volunteer Park .
Broad community resistance and pushback from families led district officials to back away from those closures .

Systemwide enrollment has now dropped from more than 94,000 students in 1964 to under 50,000 today. Shuldiner says that smaller campuses face operational challenges, including multi-grade split classrooms, solitary grade-level teachers, and limited access to full-time arts and music specialists.
There are major financial stakes to the consolidation plan.

Across the district, Seattle Public Schools has wrestled with annual deficits between $90 million and $130 million as enrollment fell below 50,000 students. In previous consolidation tries, the district estimated that shuttering an elementary campus generates roughly $750,000 to $1.5 million in annual operational savings by cutting administrative overhead, utility costs, and custodial services, while instructional staffing follows students to receiving sites.

Montlake Elementary was prepared for the changes following a nearly $80 million modernization and expansion completed in 2025. The rebuilt campus can accommodate up to 500 students, adding modern classrooms, an integrated library and cafeteria, and energy-efficient systems that replaced decades-old portable classrooms.

Beyond general elementary consolidations, Shuldiner said that the district is reviewing options for specialized programs across the city. This includes the Central District’s Seattle World School on E Union, which serves immigrant and refugee secondary students. Shuldiner said that the school itself will not be shuttered, but district leadership is exploring partnerships with one or more comprehensive high schools to strengthen its academic offerings.
The district is also evaluating site locations for its Bridges transition programs and Interagency Academy sites.

Aside from Stevens, no other neighborhood elementary schools in Capitol Hill or the Central District including Lowell, McGilvra, Leschi, Madrona, or Bailey Gatzert are being considered for closure in this round.
The changes will mean different patterns for families living in the area.

Under Seattle Public Schools student assignment rules, elementary students residing outside a one-mile “walk zone” qualify for bus transportation; however, for many families living in the Stevens area around 19th Ave E, Volunteer Park, and E Galer, the shift to Montlake’s campus at 2409 22nd Avenue E extends the commute up to 1.5 miles across a steep hill. Walking or biking routes will put more kids on busy arterials like Boyer and 24th and the Lake Washington Blvd corridor near 520. If the merger is finalized by the School Board in early 2027, the district’s transportation department will be required to run new walkshed hazard evaluations and adjust bus routing tiers.

Shuldiner took over as superintendent this year, buoyed in the role by the city’s newly approved $1.3 billion families and education levy that could provide funding for the Stevens campus to be part of expansion of programs including city-partnered early learning hubs, SPP preschool classrooms, or specialized programs like Bridges and Interagency..

In addition to the levy funding, transportation, walking, and biking concerns, Seattle City Hall may also have more to say about the proposed Stevens plan — of a more personal note. Mayor Katie Wilson has talked about living in the Stevens assignment area and her child is currently enrolled in the city-funded Seattle Preschool Program .

The new Stevens consolidation push is being rolled out for a more solid, perhaps better communicated process. The announcements come weeks before key meetings. Officials emphasized that no final decisions have been made on any site. In a joint message sent to their school communities, Stevens Principal Peter Donovan and Montlake Principal Tina Wood announced a family listening session planned for early December at Montlake Elementary.

“This work is currently in Phase 1, focused on listening, learning, and gathering feedback. No decisions have been made. Your voices, experiences, and perspectives are important as we begin these conversations,” Donovan and Wood wrote.
Under the district’s schedule, leadership and principal consultations continue through October, while meetings with school staff will run through the beginning of November.
Joint family conversations at proposed receiving sites follow throughout November and conclude in mid-December.

Once staff and family feedback is gathered, Shuldiner plans to formally present the consolidation recommendations to the Seattle School Board and the public around late December. That presentation will launch a 60-day window for public hearings and community forums in January and February, leading up to a final school board vote in late February or early March 2027.

To assist transitioning households, the district will give displaced students open enrollment transfer priority and will keep its school choice application window open until one week after the board’s final vote.

articles.title: See You at the Crossroads
articles.author: Daudi Abe, Charles Mudede
paras: For as long as music has been around, so has that phantom place beyond the crossroads, the point where life ends and the end begins. From the pre-European-encounter mbira music of Zimbabwe, which communicates with the ancestors, to Mozart’s Requiem , to Blind Willie Johnson’s utterly haunting “Dark Was the Night, Cold Was the Ground,” to the gothic movement that emerged in the late ’70s in the UK, human mortality and the great unknown called death have inspired an extraordinary range of artistic interpretations. The emergence of hip-hop, however, introduced new dimensions to this relationship, shaped by the culture’s origins, social context, and lived experiences.

Hip-hop’s birth occurred in and around urban communities shaped by socially imposed poverty, violence, and gun culture, and this dire situation, which is still with us today, resulted in a relationship between music and death that’s unique.

Hip-hop’s efforts to process grief, loss, vulnerability, and fear have often collided with the bravado, emotional restraint, and composure under pressure long associated with the culture. How does a culture that prizes strength and resilience make room for mourning? In raps that express a grief that’s profound and deeply personal. This grief is what we explore in our show, See You at the Crossroads: Death & Hip-Hop , on Thursday, October 29, at Black & Tan Hall. It was inspired by Tish Gallow, a central figure of Columbia City’s cultural life (she promotes musical South Seattle events and heads the popular Columbia City Beatwalk). This summer, she began planning an event devoted to fallen hip-hop stars, such as Phife Dawg, Biz Markie, and MCA. It’s called Tribute to Fallen Hiphop Soldiers and will happen November 20 at Columbia City Theater. As Tish celebrates fallen rappers, we reflect on the golden-era rap tracks about the grief experienced when those close to you are “dead and gone.”

That said, violence in hip-hop is as real as a heart attack. A number of famous rappers were brought down by bullets: Scott La Rock, Mac Dre, Tupac Shakur, the Notorious B.I.G., XXXTentacion, and Jam Master Jay, to name a few. But that’s not the whole story. Hip-hop is not desensitized. It can plumb the emotional depths when it comes to loss. This show is about that feeling. Let’s get down to it.

Prior to his departure from NWA, many viewed Ice Cube as the group’s lyrical consciousness. This song, from his first solo project, the EP Kill at Will , frames the discussion of friends dying within the dynamics of gangs and the drug trade. It also provides a window into the trauma associated with these events—“still hear the screams from his mother, while my n*gga lay dead in the gutter.”

Though some consider Tupac one of the great lyricists of all time, others view him as the most emotive MC hip-hop has seen. On that score, “So Many Tears” is a prime example. Children dying, tears shed, friends gone, and questions of salvation, or whether he is even worthy, frame the delivery.

This track will break your heart. It’s about a man who MC Lyte has a thing for because, to be honest, he’s fine. But he also has lots of personal problems, one of which is heavy drinking (particularly vodka). One night, he has had way too much, gets into his car, and takes his last ride (he hits a truck). The track is powerful because MC Lyte is not really judgmental. She just wishes she could have done more to help the troubled guy. The moral of her story? If you have demons, you have to face them, or they will conquer you. Poor Georgie.

In the aftermath of Geto Boys’ “Mind Playing Tricks on Me,” one of the rawest examinations of the mental toll the streets take is Scarface’s tale of a recently released ex-con who falls back into the crime life. After the man is shot during a robbery, Scarface hovers over the hospital bed while delivering chilling details of his final moments.
“Peaceful Journey” by Heavy D & the Boyz (1991)/“They Reminisce Over You (T.R.O.Y.)” by Pete Rock & CL Smooth (1992)

Two songs memorializing Troy Dixon, aka Trouble T Roy, a dancer for Heavy D who died in an accident in 1990. Though not exclusively about Dixon, the hypnotic, haunting sax loop in “T.R.O.Y.” leaves a lasting feeling of mystical spiritualism.

The coffee craze of the 1980s did not miss hip-hop. MC Lyte’s drift between life and death after being shot mirrors her before-and-after experience of drinking cappuccino. This also brings the question of whether men and women in hip-hop experience death and grief differently. (Listen to “Poor Georgie.”)
“Murder Was the Case” by Snoop Doggy Dogg (1994)
This song was also the title track to a short film of the same name. In it, Snoop is shot and killed, only to experience a supernatural resurrection after agreeing to sell his soul.
“Walkin’ 2 My Funeral” by Brotha Lynch Hung (1993)

In the early ’90s, Brotha Lynch Hung established himself as an architect of what could be termed “West Coast Horrorcore.” However, in this song, the self-described “baby killin’ atheist” introduced samples from an upbeat-sounding, melodic track (“Remind Me” by Patrice Rushen) to accompany tales of his death by police, at a dice game, and in a robbery. This idea of “Walkin’ 2 My Funeral” seems to parallel, at least conceptually, the scene from Mark Twain’s novel The Adventures of Tom Sawyer where Tom, Huck Finn, and Joe Harper crash their own memorial service.
“Grand Groove” by Intelligent Hoodlum (1993)

This is really one of the most beautiful hip-hop tracks about “living and dying,” about “losing those who are close to you.” Intelligent Hoodlum’s impeccable boom-bap flow goes deeper and deeper into an emotional space that grieves the loss of a friend who was very close to him, who was there when he needed him, who he completely trusted: “No snakes in the grass when you are near.” He misses Grand Groove to this day. He loves him to this day. And as long as he is alive, Groove will “live on and on.”
“Tha Crossroads” by Bone Thugs-N-Harmony (1995)

In 2008, the Hip Hop Reader defined the crossroads as: “The juncture of the spiritual realm and the phenomenal world. The points of literal intersection are where one might go to offer sacrifice or prayer to ancestors. The crossroads also function as a powerful symbol in African American folklore. Legends tell of Black musicians going to crossroads and trading their guitars with spirits to confirm or enhance their talents.”

Bone Thugs’ harmonic rendering of this concept again conjures a serene, spiritual feeling that underscores the topic, and the point is driven home by the Angel of Death character featured in the video.
See You at the Crossroads: Death & Hip-Hop with Charles Mudede, Daudi Abe, and DJ Vitamin D is Thurs Oct 29 at Black & Tan Hall . Get tickets here .
