articles.title: Phones and Cameras Were Banned at the Phoebe Bridgers Show
articles.author: Audrey Vann
paras: “Does anyone here have a weird relationship with their dad?” Phoebe Bridgers asked the sold-out Climate Pledge Arena on Friday night, and a wave of young voices erupted in a primal scream. Standing on a small spinning stage in the center of the crowd, Bridgers opened up about her own father. “He was… complicated,” she sighed. Although he instilled in her a love of music and leftist politics, he was often violent. “I’ve always thought that I’d rather die than be like that,” she said. “But then he died, and I felt a flood of empathy. That’s obviously what Lost Weekend is about.” Because of the album’s content, Bridgers shared that it was both unsettling to write and even more challenging to perform. “Eliminating cell phones on this tour was initially just a way for me to mitigate my fear of singing these songs live,” she explained, “but it turned out to be one of the most enjoyable experiences of my life.”

This no-phone/no-photography policy was the reason that my date for the evening was retired courtroom sketch artist Doug Keith . Since we always include photos with our live show reviews, I became fixated on the idea of hiring a professional sketch artist to cover the show with me and provide the imagery. I had seen fan-made art from the shows circulating on social media; would an artist—one who’s been trained to capture the energy of a scene—be able to document an arena concert? I searched “Seattle courtroom sketch artist” online and found an article mentioning Keith, who worked as a freelance sketch artist documenting trials for KIRO-TV, KOMO News, the Seattle Times , and more, back in the 1980s, even winning an Emmy for graphic design in 1982 at KIRO-TV. He appeared to be retired from courtroom depiction but was an active children’s book illustrator and garden art sculptor, with several other endeavors like museum dressing, custom-painted guitars, and playing in a band himself. When I nervously cold-called Keith to see if he was interested, he not only seemed enthusiastic about the idea, but also was familiar with Bridgers’s music (he likes “Motion Sickness”).

Keith and I arrived at the arena together right as the doors opened. As we waited in line for security, he remarked that he was probably the oldest person at the concert. There were times when I felt guilty for taking him on this adventure: seeing the large crowds and price-gouged snacks through his eyes made me realize just how much discomfort we accept in order to see our favorite pop stars. Keith and I fumbled through security—my bag was too big but they let me in anyway. Something in Keith’s pocket kept sounding the alarm (I realized later that it was his pencil sharpener). We said goodbye to our cellphones and locked them into little fabric bags called Yondr Pouches, secured with a magnetic lock that only employees could open. Inside, we were immediately met with a monstrous merch line and no place to put ourselves back together after the security fiasco. We made our way downstairs, where Keith found a standing table near the concession stand. He took out his sketchbook, pencils, and pastels, and began to capture fan costumes while I got in the merch line to buy my sister a gift.

The two merch lines on the second floor were so long that the ends of the lines briefly kissed. A girl in front of me flapped around her Yondr Pouch to the beat of an indie rock song that I couldn’t identify. The couple behind me fondled leaves on the plant wall and debated whether or not the foliage was real. At least a dozen young women wearing boygenius-style dress shirts and ties passed me—something I realized I hadn’t seen since the Avril Lavigne concert at Southcenter Mall in 2004. I also saw many different takes on Bridgers’s famous skeleton suit: bedazzled bone T-shirts, cozy-looking jumpsuits, and crocheted vests. There were almost too many alien antenna headbands to count. Elf ears were also popular. Perhaps the most impressive were the three separate people I saw dressed in full ghost sheets with the eyes cut out, replicating the Stranger in the Alps album cover. Niche costumes also appeared that I couldn’t identify: fuzzy red fox ears and tail, a full-body taco costume, and someone who painted their entire face blue.

I returned to Keith’s table with two beers and he cracked one open, remarking, “I could never drink a beer in my courtroom days.” All the waiting around gave me plenty of time to ask Keith about those days. He recalled being hired to sketch during a 1985 indictment of 10 (out of 23) neo-Nazis : “Each one of them had a lawyer, so it was like drawing the Sistine Chapel!” Keith also remembered a chilling moment when a convicted murderer, who he recalls being the last person in Washington to be sentenced to death by hanging— Charles Rodman Campbell —stared at him intensely while he sketched. “That guy was a real creep.”

We made our way through the tightly packed crowds to find our seats—a challenge, considering the arena was completely dark aside from thin sticks of light that surrounded opener Alex G in the center of the crowd. Something I had not considered about the presence of cell phones at concerts was how much light they emit. It then dawned on me that in movie theaters, opera productions, and Broadway shows, no-phone spaces don’t just eliminate distraction, but black out the rest of the world and allow the audience to escape their lives and put their full attention into the art in front of them a little bit.

While we waited for Phoebe, I watched the people around me play with lighters and ponder their Yondr Pouches. Without phones, we were eventually forced to entertain ourselves the old-fashioned way: talking to one another. The person in front of me showed me their merch haul. Sitting beside me was a fellow writer and his daughter—we discussed the best shows we’ve seen this year and our process for writing reviews. Eventually, someone in the crowd started a wave, and it circled around the arena at least a dozen times before arms got tired and it fizzled out.

Then, the lights shut off again. The giant igloo on the stage lit up. We heard Bridgers’s voice singing “The Outside,” but we couldn’t see where she was. “Is she going to be lifted down from the ceiling?” Keith asked me jokingly. The igloo then opened like a clamshell to reveal Bridgers in her full Hitchcock heroine beauty—perfectly waved platinum hair, a black minidress, and tears painted on with silver glitter. “What the fuck is up, Seattle!?” she screamed into the microphone. Fans roared Beatlemania-style as Bridgers went into “Motion Sickness.”

From the moment that Bridgers arrived onstage, I could see that this was a comically bad environment for drawing. Everyone stood up out of their seats, which made it impossible for Keith to sit and sketch. The lighting in the arena went from complete darkness to bright bursts of house lights. My eyes were struggling to adjust, and I knew Keith was experiencing the same. A close-up of Bridgers was projected in black and white on a curtain behind the stage, which could have been helpful if it weren’t for all the creases in the fabric that warped her image. All of this made for an amazing live spectacle, but an impossible drawing subject. “I could draw this guy,” Keith joked, pointing at the man standing in front of him who was blocking his view. Realizing that this was an absurd task, I encouraged Keith to put his sketch pad down and just enjoy the show, but he didn’t give up and completed two sketches of Bridgers by the end of the night.

Throughout the show, Bridgers moved back and forth from the main stage to a smaller B-stage, often by physically walking through the crowd greeting fans. On the B-stage, which slowly spun in the center of the pit, Bridgers sat cross-legged on the floor while playing an organ, then played an acoustic guitar beneath a UFO-like ray of light. As she sang the emotional “Still Standing,” fake snow and glittering sparklers fell around her.

Back on the main stage, Bridgers returned to her igloo. “I love introducing people to bands they wouldn’t hear about otherwise,” she said sarcastically. “This is Nirvana… you guys should check them out.” She then explained that the last time she sang this song was two months ago for BBC Radio 1, during which her appendix was “actively bursting” while she sang. “Hopefully nothing bad happens this time!” Bridgers’s rendition of the song was stunningly quiet and folk-influenced, bringing to mind Elliott Smith’s prolific live covers .

During her last song, “Scott Street,” a circular chain of young women began to dance down in the pit. Hundreds of fans held up paper hearts made of blue, green, and purple construction paper. Phoebe asked who coordinated the hearts and thanked the leader. She then graciously thanked the crowd for coming out and walked off the stage with no encores or fancy gimmicks (I love to see it!). I was struck by just how refreshingly authentic and in-the-moment she seemed—making jokes and connecting with the audience about childhood trauma and grief—compared to other pop stars, who are typically meticulously scripted and choreographed. I assume this is largely because they are aware that every move will be recorded and later scrutinized on social media. Without the looming presence of phones, Bridgers played the 17k+ crowd with the ease and freedom of a house show.

Exiting the show was another series of obstacles for me and Keith—leaving our seats was like trying to get off an airplane with people competing for a spot in the aisle, as was getting on the escalator to the main exit. We waited in line for our phones to be released, then waited again to leave the parking lot. Finally, close to midnight, I was headed back to Keith’s house to drop him off, where I learned how he met his wife, Beth (she asked him for a cigarette at a dance club in the 1980s), and we commiserated about having partners who don’t drive (hell hath no fury like a lifelong designated driver!). Although we shared disappointment about the circumstances for drawing at the concert, I came to realize that this project wasn’t about finding an alternative to the camera phone, but about embracing humanity and the joy and connection sparked from doing things the hard way.

articles.title: Stranger Suggests: Your Agenda This Week, October 26–November 1
articles.author: Julianne Bell, Shannon Lubetich, Megan Seling, and Audrey Vann
paras: (MUSIC) Wanna feel old? It’s been 10 years since Greta Kline, aka Frankie Cosmos, released her 2016 studio album Next Thing , which contains some of her most well-known songs, including “Fool,” “Sappho,” and “Outside With the Cuties.” The dreamy, wistful record features influences from poet Frank O’Hara and musician Arthur Russell, with Kline’s floaty vocals and contemplative lyrics layered over soft synths. It packs the emotional punch of a coming-of-age film into the span of 28 minutes and 28 seconds and defined my 20s—in fact, I am having an existential spiral realizing that it’s been a decade since I attended the Vera Project show for Frankie Cosmos’s West Coast tour promoting this album alongside former Seattle favorites iji (now based in Los Angeles). Kline and her band will return to Seattle to celebrate Next Thing ’s anniversary at the Crocodile, with an opening set by hometown heroes Coral Grief, and I fully expect it to heal me. ( Crocodile, 8 pm, all ages ) JULIANNE BELL

(MUSIC) I’ve been a fan of Dolly Parton’s spiritual successor Kacey Musgraves since her 2013 single “Follow Your Arrow,” and it’s been a treat to watch her career evolve over the years. Her bittersweet latest album, Middle of Nowhere , finds her deep in her single era, evoking both liminal spaces and her Texan roots—the title comes from a sign she spotted in her hometown that read, “​​Golden, Texas: Somewhere in the middle of nowhere.” It’s by turns horny, as on the touch-starved bop “Dry Spell” (“Ain’t nobody’s tool up in my shed / Ain’t nobody’s boots under my bed”), and heartbreaking, as on the ballad “Hell on Me.” She also works out a 15-year feud with country star Miranda Lambert on the remix in their duet “Horses and Divorces”: “It’s all whiskey under the bridge.” Seattle-based sibling busker trio the Brudi Brothers will kick off Musgraves’s show at Climate Pledge Arena. ( Climate Pledge Arena, 7:30 pm, all ages ) JULIANNE BELL

(FOOD) Sure, it’s confusing that Seattle Restaurant Week is actually two weeks, but that just means we have twice as much time to pig out on specials from dozens of delicious participating restaurants. And there are some true superstars on the list. Lupe’s Situ Tacos in Ballard will be offering a few different specials, including three of their incredibly crispy tacos, or five taquitos, served alongside a cup of soup, aguas frescas, and baklava for $30. That’s enough food for two! (Though I do hate to share my taquitos.) There’s also Shiro’s Sushi, Marination in Columbia City (and, hell yeah, their special includes malasadas), Kilig, which Stranger contributor Meg van Huygen put on her 2024 Best Restaurants in the Seattle Area list, and Melting Pot in Bellevue. I did not know Melting Pot still existed! The ’90s really are back. (Various locations) MEGAN SELING

(MUSIC) I’m hard-pressed to think of many artists who reinvent themselves as effortlessly and confidently as Beatrice Laus, better known by her stage name beabadoobee. The Filipino British singer-songwriter rose to fame with her debut single, “Coffee,” which went viral on YouTube in 2017 and blew up even more after it was sampled on Canadian rapper ​​Powfu’s TikTok-popular 2019 song “Death Bed (Coffee for Your Head).” Two years after her indie-pop album This Is How Tomorrow Moves , she’s adopting an edgier, grungier sound with her new album Pylon , which incorporates ’90s alt influences and enlists Hayley Williams, Pinegrove’s Evan Stephens Hall, Deftones’ Chino Moreno, and Turnstile’s Brendan Yates as collaborators. Laus’s ethereal vocals recall the Cranberries’ Dolores O’Riordan over fuzzy, shoegaze-tinged guitars, simmering with heartbreak and nostalgia—the album gets its title from the pylon towers she’d gaze at out the window while homesick on tour. Up-and-coming nu-gaze artist Wisp will join her on her first arena tour. ( Climate Pledge, 8 pm, all ages ) JULIANNE BELL

(MUSIC) Rebecca Black has successfully shed the skin of her notoriously cringe viral bop “Friday.” Today, her public persona leans into her status as a queer icon, hyperpop sensation, and collaborator of genre rule-breakers like Dylan Brady (100 gecs), Big Freedia, and Dorian Electra. On her sophomore album, Age of the Exhibitionist , she harmonizes about kink and pleasure à la Madonna’s Erotica . Explaining to Out Magazine her hopes for the album, Black said, “I hope [listeners] sweat, I hope they fuck, I hope they do everything they need to do. There really is a song for everything on this record.” Brooklyn-based artist BAYLI will open with her signature blend of club, rap, and pop bangers. ( Showbox, 7 pm, all ages ) AUDREY VANN

(PARTY) Break out your black eyeliner and pleather pants; it’s time for Southgate Roller Rink’s Goth Skate and Halloween party. You can bring your own skates or grab rentals to join goblins, ghouls, fairies, princesses, and other costumed characters out on the rink while DJs, bands, drag artists, and go-gos perform on two different stages. The live music lineup is stacked with Heebie Jeebies’ surf-punk takes of Halloween classics, the Holy Divers of Babylon’s heavy metal tribute, the Band That Ate My Brain’s punk covers, Ghosts in the Graveyard’s theatrical deathrock, and Neuroprison’s post-punk darkwave tunes. If thrills are what you seek, head out to the beer garden for a hair-raising haunted house. ( Southgate Roller Rink, 9 pm, 21+ ) SHANNON LUBETICH

(MUSIC) English singer-songwriter Patrick Wolf got his start playing viola for artists like Arcade Fire and CocoRosie while working on solo music in the early aughts. After a decade grinding in the industry and experiencing some personal setbacks, Wolf took a step back from music, returning to the scene with a new EP in 2023. With fans from Lady Gaga to Tilda Swinton (who narrated a documentary about his life that came out earlier this year), the musician makes dark and theatrical songs perfect for Halloween weekend, incorporating influences from chamber pop, folk, electronica, and gothic rock. Wolf taps Hollow Eve, who starred in the Boulet Brothers’ Emmy-nominated show Dragula , to open the night with their “unbridled mediumship of the divine and grotesque.” ( Tractor Tavern, 8 pm, 21+ ) SHANNON LUBETICH

articles.title: Op-Ed: Stop MAGA from Taking Over Washington, Vote No on I-645, I-001, and I-638
articles.author: Suresh Chanmugam
paras: I was born and raised in Baton Rouge, Louisiana to immigrant parents. I moved to Seattle in 1999 to work as a software engineer in large part due to the progressive values cultivated by Washington State. My wife and I are grateful to the communities and culture here, where we’ve been able to raise three children who attend public schools in diverse communities. One of the reasons we are raising our kids here is Washington’s commitment to inclusion. Our state was one of the first to pass marriage equality, and we have strong laws against discrimination.

I deeply appreciate that the tech industry in Washington is considered a safe, welcoming place for LGBTQIA+ people, particularly our transgender friends and colleagues, who face escalating threats to their very right to existence. More parents, including many of our tech colleagues, say they are moving here to protect their children from draconian laws that are linked to increases in suicide rates.

But, near-trillionaire Elon Musk is fanning the flames against the transgender community by spending hundreds of millions of dollars through his “America PAC” (political action committee) running anti-trans political ads in elections around the country to try to drive swing voters to vote Republican. Most voters agree that this strategy is using hate to try to distract us from the high cost of groceries, gas, housing, and healthcare.

Now, right here in blue Washington State, multi-millionaire hedge fund manager Brian Heywood, through his PAC Let’s Go Washington, is using the same MAGA playbook. Heywood and his posse of right-wing uber rich supporters are bankrolling three harmful ballot measures before Washington voters this election, and two of them put a target on the backs of LGBTQIA+ children, a particularly malicious tactic.

Initiative 638 (IL26-638 on your ballot) is the most extreme policy of its kind in the country, and that’s saying a lot when red states like Idaho, Florida, Tennessee, Kansas, Utah, and Iowa have passed dozens of laws restricting civil rights, freedoms and access to care for transgender people. To exclude and humiliate trans girls from sports, I-638 would require all girls to undergo sex inspections to play elementary, middle, or high school sports.

Doctors say to be in compliance with this new rule, they will have to conduct invasive genital exams on young girls or expensive genetic and hormone testing that is unlikely to be covered by insurance because it is not medically-necessary. (And in blatant discrimination, only girls would be required to undergo potentially harmful sex inspections because the initiative exempts boys.)

Initiative 001 (IL26-001) is an anti-parents rights, anti-LGBTQIA+ measure. As a parent of three Seattle Public Schools teenagers, I know the facts: parents already have the right to information about their child, including the right to opt them out of certain curriculum or programs, and to talk to teachers, school counselors or nurses about their concerns.

While most kids have a safe loving home, sadly not all do. There were more than 115,000 reports of child abuse in Washington state in 2024 alone. As someone deeply involved with work to address our housing crisis, I have seen that the majority of homeless youth are LGBTQIA+ kids who have been kicked out or left their home because they didn’t feel safe there. I-001 will make this crisis worse, and is a direct threat to the safety of vulnerable young children who need confidential access to trusted, trained professionals like school counselors.

Initiative 645 (IP26-645) is an extension of Musk and the billionaire bros who successfully lobbied the Trump administration for policies that benefit themselves, Heywood is also trying to buy a tax cut for himself and other extremely wealthy individuals by repealing Washington’s new millionaires tax. The tax itself is very popular with the majority of voters in part because it pays for B&O tax cuts for small businesses (including small tech startups) and cuts the regressive sales taxes that impact working families. It raises billions for schools, childcare, free meals for K-12 students, and tax rebates for working families.

Having grown up in Louisiana, a state notorious for underfunded public schools, it’s appalling to me that Washington’s public school system isn’t much better. Our schools are chronically underfunded due to our state’s upside down tax code and I-645 will make it worse.

I’m tired of the false narrative that workers and businesses are leaving the state because of the millionaires tax. Skilled workers don’t want to leave Washington and move to Tennessee or Texas where they could face jail time and even death because they had a miscarriage. In fact, Starbucks, Oracle, and others have struggled to convince their employees to leave Washington. Over 100 Seattle Starbucks employees chose to have their job eliminated rather than move their family to a red state. Oracle moved its headquarters to Nashville and added only seven net new employees there last year. Austin is declining as a tech hub.

The Seattle metro region is the second largest tech hub in the country, but passing these initiatives would risk a tech talent flight to communities with stronger human rights protections like the Bay Area, New York City, Boston, and Northern Virginia. Political initiatives like I-645, I-001, and I-638 aren't just harmful to marginalized members of our community; they're also bad for business.

I urge my tech colleagues to say no to Brian Heywood and his attempt to distract us from the real problems caused by MAGA politicians, like exorbitant groceries, escalating rents, disappearing health care, and a reckless war that has killed innocent civilians and caused permanent destruction of business data that was supposed to have 99.999999999% (11 nines) of durability . Rejecting Heywood’s initiatives is one way we can protect all children’s rights, health, safety, educational, and economic opportunities.
Suresh Chanmugam has worked as a software engineer in Seattle since 1999 and is a steering committee member of Tech 4 Housing .
Editor's note: The Urbanist Elections Committee also endorsed a "no" vote on Initiatives 001, 638, and 645 .

articles.title: Op-Ed: Prop 1 Will Sustain Seattle's Transit Momentum
articles.author: Ashwin Bhumbla
paras: It cost me three dollars to get to City Hall the day I joined many others to fight for the future of Seattle transit. An Uber would have been a little faster but much more expensive at twenty dollars. I could've used a Lime bike, but it would've taken longer and, again, would have been more expensive at around fifteen dollars. Maybe I could've driven, but like 20% of households in Seattle , I don't own a car. I shudder to think how much purchasing one for that drive would've set me back.

So, I left the cafe I was working from and despite having recently missed a bus, I had to wait only seven minutes until the next one arrived. I hopped on the Route 7 and in about twenty minutes I was at City Hall along with dozens of others to advocate for a strong Seattle Transit Measure renewal in front of City Council . The trip was affordable, safe, fast, and easy.

After listening to over an hour of public testimony, it was clear that transit advocacy was only scratching the surface of reasons folks relied on the bus. I heard workers in tech, healthcare, service, public works, manufacturing, and trade describe the route they relied on to get to work. I heard seniors who could not afford to or who were unable to drive speak glowingly of the bus that took them to groceries, healthcare visits, and to resource centers. I heard union workers speak to what working for the transit system meant to them and their families. Speaker after speaker remarked on how they would not be able to afford to get to the places they needed to go without the bus. Finally, I heard a commenter describe how they relied on the bus for love, taking it to a first date – drawing the loudest cheer from the crowd of the day.

The advocacy that day succeeded. The measure we were fighting for survived being watered down and is now on your ballots. For a more affordable, sustainable, and accessible city, and for every person, I heard that day, and in the many days since, I’m voting yes on Proposition 1 to renew the Seattle Transit Measure and to expand and improve our incredible transit system.

Before asking you to do the same, perhaps some background context would be helpful. The Seattle Transit Measure (STM) renewal will authorize the city to collect a 0.3% sales tax for 10 years, collecting approximately $138 million annually. This is an increase from the current STM which is a six year sales tax (2020 to 2026) at a 0.15% sales tax rate, generating around $50 million annually. These funds will be spent on a variety of transit-related investments, but will be primarily used to bolster bus service in Seattle.

I believe passing this measure will improve the lives of every Seattleite. I have faith in this prediction as the best predictor of the future is the past, and by every metric, the current STM has been a massive success. It passed in 2020 with a staggering 80% of the vote! But its electoral success does not matter as much as what it actually did . The enormous faith voters placed in the measure has more than paid off, and renewing the measure will continue to build on that momentum. We can see this by breaking down what that money was spent on and what it achieved.

While bus service is provided by King County Metro and thus funded by a county-wide 0.9% sales tax, demand for transit service in Seattle has been higher than the baseline service Metro provides. This is the primary reason why the Seattle Transit Measure was first passed in 2014, passed again overwhelmingly in 2020, and why it should be approved again now.

One out of every 15 buses (approximately 180,000 annual trips) that run in Seattle are currently funded by the STM. That is a massive amount of trips that the STM has delivered every year of its existence.

More buses are better for everyone. For transit riders, increased frequency and reliability means more flexibility and less stress. Frequency is freedom and expanding when and how often a bus runs makes transit more viable as a primary mode of transportation. That makes things better even for drivers as the more people that take the bus– with fewer driving cars, the roads will be safer and less traffic-heavy.

Finally, more transit service is a necessity. From a sustainability standpoint, reducing the total number of vehicles on the road is the single most impactful thing our city can do to reduce its emissions. From a logistics standpoint, the city keeps growing, adding thousands to its population every year. However, we have limited street space. There simply is not room to add more cars to this city at the rate people currently drive. To continue Seattle's growth, we need to make transit a more viable mode of transportation. The current STM has made enormous strides in this regard. Unfortunately, it's still not enough.

Seattle wants more transit service because it needs more transit service. Due to funding issues caused by the Covid-19 pandemic as well as funding and operator availability issues from King County Metro, total bus service is actually at a lower level than it was pre-pandemic in 2019. We are down from 70% of the city having access to ten minute frequency service to approximately 53% . Transit demand has shifted, no longer only commute-based, but also with greater demand being seen for increased frequency on weekends, evenings, and nights. Late night service remains sparse. SDOT's Frequent Transit Network (FTN) , its aspirational goal in service of addressing these shortcomings, is still not fulfilled.

This is where the STM renewal comes into play. The renewal, with its increased funding, will almost double the amount of bus trips added by the current STM, going up to 275,000 trips added annually. It will focus on filling gaps in the FTN, adding additional trips on key routes on off-peak hours. Seattle is a city that does not only exist to go to work and this measure will help make transit a more viable option for every transportation need at all times of the day.

Seattle residents won’t have to wait years to see the benefits. If this measure passes, these additional trips will be phased in relatively quickly as part of Metro's twice-yearly service changes. Metro has confirmed that it is coming out of the operator shortage it has been facing the past few years and stands ready to not only increase its baseline level of service but also fulfill the additional trips that Seattle would be purchasing should STM be renewed. Every additional bus trip funded means that the most affordable transportation option becomes more viable for more people.

It's also important to note that King County Metro, as the operator of the buses, is most directly responsible for safety and security on those buses. By purchasing all this additional bus service, a portion of every transit service purchase goes directly to Metro's safety and security programming. In 2025, 6.3% of STM funds were spent on Metro's safety initiatives. The renewal, by increasing investment in bus service, will continue and expand this investment and continue to make the safest mode of transportation even safer.

On top of bus service, the STM has funding for capital projects to unlock more transit service and make it safer and more reliable. The current STM funded projects such as adding bus lanes on Rainier Ave (which increased performance for riders of the Routes 7, 48, and 106) or contributing funding to the RapidRide J line. While not directly funded by the STM, the recent Denny Way Bus Reliability Project , is another example of the immediate relief that targeted capital projects can provide, having quickly and effectively improved the reliability of both the Route 8 bus. The STM renewal will continue to have funding for capital projects such as these to ensure that buses can run faster, making every dollar invested in transit service go farther.

The current STM also expands access to transit by ensuring that those who need assistance the most can afford to use it. Through the Transportation Access Programs (TAP), STM currently provides around 10,000 free ORCA cards for residents of Seattle Housing Authority, Seattle Promise Scholars, and Seattle Preschool Program families who attend tuition free.

The STM renewal would more than double the amount of ORCA card recipients, going to 22,000 total. While transit is already vastly more affordable than owning and operating a personal car ( which now costs an average annual amount of over twelve thousand dollars nationwide and shows no sign of decreasing, as gas prices continue to climb), there are still many in this city to whom the cost is a barrier. STM and its renewal do not only expand transit, they expand access to transit, which is just as essential.

While buses consist of the majority of transit investments, the STM also funds essential transit services such as the First Hill and South Lake Union Streetcars, Trailhead Direct, and on-demand Metro Flex services.
The STM renewal will continue these investments to ensure that transit access is spread as far as possible.

The STM is a great piece of legislation. It has delivered immediate returns to the taxpayers that overwhelmingly voted it in and its renewal will make its investments even stronger. Investing in stronger, more accessible transit service pays dividends for affordability, safety, livability, and local economy. The more people can afford to safely get where they live and work and play, the better our city becomes.

The impact of an increase to an already high local sales tax cannot be ignored. Unfortunately, until state law changes, sales tax is the most viable method of funding transit service. The STM renewal and its increase of 0.15% to the sales tax rate would be estimated to cost the average Seattle median two-person household an additional $29 per year - even less for many single-person and lower-income households. In an earlier op-ed , the MASS coalition put this cost into context by comparing it to 4 hours of parking, one hour of riding a Lime, a 30 minute uber, a tank of gas, or one week of car ownership.

The purpose of such a comparison is not to make light of what a tax increase means to people at a time where every dollar needs to go the furthest it possibly can. On the contrary, the comparison shows what a good investment the STM renewal truly is and how affordable investment in transit is when compared to other transportation options. If we do not renew the STM, we will face drastic guaranteed transit service cuts. The hit to transit service and the increased cost of relying more on other modes of transportation will far outweigh the cost of the measure.

Seattle is a world-class city with world-class transit, but it can be even better. Good public transit is not free, but it does bring freedom. Freedom to work, to shop, to seek help, to play; freedom from traffic and from never-ending car payments. Transit connects our city and connects people to the places they need to access in order to live their lives.

Sometimes in this city there is a sense that the Seattle Process™ can overwhelm us, slow things down, make it seem like actually changing anything is impossible. That building things is no longer feasible.

We can build, and not only that, we can build quickly and efficiently. Should the STM be renewed, its benefits will not potentially be felt a decade from now. It will be felt within months. Whether you are an avid transit user, driver, both, neither, or anywhere in between, vote Yes on Proposition 1 to renew the Seattle Transit Measure and help build our transit network to make this city more affordable, safe, and easy to navigate.

articles.title: Downtown Highrise Project Still Under Fire as Design Gets Revised Taller
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The property owners behind a potential cross-laminated timber highrise project in Downtown Seattle aren't shirking away in response to considerable pushback against their project – they're going taller. Plans shown this week to the Seattle Landmarks Board would still add a residential tower above a retrofitted Doyle Building at 2nd Avenue and Pine Street, but include six more floors than a proposal initially floated last year .

That change is only likely to intensify opposition to the project, with preservation advocates wary of seeing significant changes to the landmarked 1920 structure joining forces with nearby condo owners not happy about seeing a new tower creep up next door. If built, the new structure would extend 23 stories up alongside its neighbor, the 39-story 1521 2nd Avenue building.

Fana Group, which owns the Doyle Building, has enlisted a team that calls itself Buildings Reimagined – made up of the design firm Clark/Barnes and general contractor BN Builders – to rethink the future of the four-story structure. The Doyle would be converted into a concrete structure capable of supporting a mass-timber tower above, retaining only the north and east facades. A one-story gasket level would accommodate the transition to 18 stories above.

Thanks to a 2025 change in state law , Washington cities can no longer require facade modulation or upper level setbacks with mass-timber developments projects or redevelopments that convert commercial space into residential. That means Seattle's existing tower spacing rules do not apply here, with an average distance to the 1521 2nd Avenue building of just under 21 feet. It also means that there are no variances being proposed by Clark/Barnes that could add additional red tape, with the landmarks approval process one of the only remaining barriers standing in the way of potential approval.

"By combining the preservation, the sustainable materials, innovative design, and construction talent, we're going to be able to add more housing downtown," W. Scott Clark of Clark/Barnes told the landmarks board Wednesday. "This is why we created Buildings Reimagined, to help distressed properties that are really challenged and also difficult to entitle, to demonstrate that preservation and financially viable development are not mutually exclusive, and that that they can benefit one another."

Historic preservation advocates apparently disagree. A group called "Save the Historic Doyle Landmark" has already sprouted up to oppose the project as presented, and the advocacy non-profit Historic Seattle sent out an action alert in advance of this week's meeting.

"While not a large or tall structure, the Doyle building has stood out through the decades as downtown has evolved, bearing witness to and surviving the boom-and-bust nature of this city. This human-scale, right-size, mixed-use building stands today due to its original high quality of design, construction, materials, condition, and integrity," Historic Seattle's email stated. "The proposal is to demolish most of the building, leaving only two facades standing, and erecting 23-stories of new residential construction behind the two facades. Let’s be clear. This is NOT an addition to a landmark. This is NOT adaptive reuse. This is NOT historic preservation. This IS facadism. If approved, this would be a demolition of most of the landmark."
But Clark pushed back on claims that they would be demolishing the Doyle this week, framing that as misinformation.

"We are not demolishing the building. We are keeping the two historic featured elevations on the two streets. [...] We are demolishing the alley facade and the roof, and we are going in and we're completely restructuring the interior of this building," Clark said. "Whether you're doing a one-story addition or a taller addition, you would need to reinforce the building to meet seismic. But given the loads that we're going to be subject to, we are going in and we're completely restructuring the internal of the building with a concrete structure."

One point of contention at the Landmarks Board is likely to be the massing of the upper story additions, which are only set back from the Doyle Building's cornices by about three-and-a-half feet. Multiple board members expressed concerns about this, especially as it relates to criteria set by the U.S. Secretary of the Interior on rehabilitation of historic structures. Criteria #9 states that new additions "will be differentiated from the old and will be compatible with the historic materials, features, size, scale and proportion, and massing" compared to the existing structure."

"What I've heard is that this has been scaled and designed to work with economics and making finances work. So as it stands, I have a lot of trouble supporting the project moving forward based on criteria number nine, and seeing that none of that has been applied to this project," board member Matthew Zinski said, referencing the gasket floor intended to be a break between the two segments of building. "Landmarks Board member Matthew Zinski said. "I struggle to see the design logic or what's being used there to help differentiate what's going on between the new addition and the existing building."
Clark defended the choice to extend the addition as far out as it's proposed, noting the limitations that are inherent on the site.

"I do have to say that we were dealing with the reality of a small [floor]plate. It's 8,900 square feet, and secondly, we had to deal with the condition of an eccentric core location, just given the overall dimensions and depths of the plate," Clark said. "We wanted to ensure that our unit layouts had the depth necessary to make comfortable living units, and so all of those things, all those very practical things, in conjunction with the vertical load path that we're trying to run through the building, in coordination with the structure, the existing structure of the landmark building really started to describe the overall mass and form of the building."
Board member Dan Sloat echoed concerns around the addition being too bulky.

"I really appreciate your discussion about the attempt to keep the the new tower structure visually quiet to create that contrast, and I think for me, the kind of equal proportioning of two parts fights against that a little bit," Sloat told Clark. "I'm having a hard time reading the visual quietness of the superstructure because it is so dimensionally similar to the structure below."

Wednesday's briefing, coming more than a year after the firm's first discussion with the Landmarks Board, still represents the early stages of the project. But the design team is heading toward applying for a Master Use Permit with the city, and is advancing forward. In the months ahead it will become clear just how much of an uphill battle getting final approval of the Landmarks Board will be.
But Clark clearly sees the project as a major benefit to downtown Seattle as a whole.

"[The Doyle building] really is at a crossroads, and we think what we're proposing is a very strong, responsible, and reasonable approach to revitalize the building and provide the needed housing downtown," Clark said.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Vote Yes on Prop 1 for More Buses!
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: Ballots for the November election have been sent to voters in King County. One item on the ballot for voters in Seattle is Proposition 1: Seattle Transit Measure. This renews and expands the Seattle Transit Measure that is set to expire in early 2027. The 0.3% sales tax is expected to generate $138 million per year that will fund 280,000 bus trips in Seattle each year for 10 years, 100,000 more bus trips than currently funded. It would also fund 22,000 free ORCA cards for low-income, elderly, and families with young children, maintain support for Seattle’s streetcar lines, fund spot improvements to keep buses moving, and help expedite permits and inspections for Link expansion projects in Seattle. Vote Yes to help fund transit in Seattle.

Since 2014, the Seattle Transit Measure has funded millions of bus trips in Seattle. Many of these trips are on weekends when most routes have less frequent service compared to weekdays. Route 36 is one such route that has received additional weekend trips. Between 2022 and 2026, the STM funded 22 additional trips on Saturdays and 42 additional trips on Sunday. In response, more people use Route 36 every weekend. Compared to 2022, Route 36 ridership on Saturday and Sunday has increased by 41% and 58%, respectively. Weekday ridership has increased 32%. This increased ridership represents more car-free trips and improved access to get to work, shops, and fun for people in Beacon Hill, Othello, and the International District.

The Route 36 success story is not an isolated one. Passengers on routes around Seatttle have benefited from additional service funded by the Seattle Transit Measure. Vote Yes to continue and expand the additional bus trips. Fill out your ballot soon and drop it off at one of the many ballot drop boxes in King County.

articles.title: Route 545 doesn’t save as much time as you think
articles.author: Alex Kvenvolden
paras: Much like route 550 was to Bellevue, route 545 has been Redmond’s workhorse route. Redmond has a diverse set of transit options fanning out in every direction, even before it had the distinction of being a Link terminus. But the main regional service has always been route 545, which connects downtown Redmond to downtown Seattle. However, as with many ST express corridors, route 545 was intended to be an interim service until rail reaches Redmond. Route 545 was always planned on being discontinued with the start of East Link service to Seattle, with the 2 Line taking over the entirety of both routes 545 and 550. The original plan (developed as part of the first iteration of King County Metro’s East Link Connections plan) deleted the 545 and 550, with some of the freed up service hours being used to make the 542 frequent and replace 545 service to Bear Creek P&R. Route 554 (later renumbered 556) was also planned to be moved to Bellevue to fill a gap in service on Bellevue Way left by the removal of route 550. Former riders of these routes either take a more frequent bus to connect the 2 Line, or can just take the 2 Line on its own.

Sound transit first let riders formally have a say on the potential changes in early 2025 as part of their 2026 service plan, and have a say they did! They received more feedback on route 545 than any other route by far, with its feedback results showing about 14% of respondents providing feedback on route 545, the runner-up being route 550 with about 9%. The broad consensus of the feedback was clear: don’t delete route 545. Sound Transit was so moved by these results that they did not even propose any changes to route 545 at all in any of their own ST Express proposals, even while moving forward with major changes nearby such as deleting route 550 and combining route 554 with route 556, relying entirely on Link to get I-90 riders to Seattle.

The reasoning is sensible. The 2 Line crosses the lake along I-90, so buses heading to Seattle via I-90 are the most duplicative of rail, and forcing a transfer would add little travel time (or even save time in some cases). Route 545, on the other hand, has a straight shot to downtown Seattle via the 520 bridge. Trading that for a detour to I-90 through Bellevue would add travel time, and riders told Sound Transit that this additional travel time isn’t acceptable. So when planning the 2026 ST Express network, Sound Transit decided to keep buses when travel times by cutting them would exceed 10 minutes (per The Urbanist , reporting from Sound Transit’s Director of System and Service Planning, Emily Yasukochi).

In keeping with the feedback they received, Sound Transit’s eventual plan had routes 545 and 542 in the “no changes” column. Here are the resulting service frequencies as they took effect late last month:

During the week, riders will continue to have frequent service on route 545, but riders heading to UW or farther north opting to use the 542 will have no frequent service at any time. Missing a 542 could make taking the 2 Line all the around through Bellevue, Mercer Island, and downtown Seattle be a faster way to get to UW just because of the 30 minute wait. Worse yet, neither the 542 or 545 are frequent on weekends, making riders who have a faster trip have to decide between a fast but infrequent bus, or a frequent but circuitous train. By comparison, route 556 (which replaces route 554 and connects Issaquah to the 2 Line) sees frequent service every day of the week, and is also more usable for intra-eastside trips (e.g., Issaquah to Bellevue or Redmond) than route 554 was.

As part of its reporting on its proposals in the 2026 service plan, Sound Transit did an analysis of travel times on routes which were to be modified in 2026. Below is its analysis, which includes some popular trips which were made on routes 522, 550, 554, 556, 574, and 586 before the 2026 changes. They estimated travel times on these trips before the 2026 service changes (labeled “current”), and did the same estimate for travel times after the service changes (labeled “future”), under the new network. The final column gives an estimated additional travel time for each trip after the 2026 changes, with negative values indicating a quicker trip.
Per the rest of the document, these estimates are calculated by adding:

With Sound Transit being selective about which changes were made, it’s unsurprising that most of these trips saw a travel time decrease, with only Issaquah TC- downtown Seattle being slower in every case. More to the point, in all cases but one, additional travel time is less than the 10 minute threshold Sound Transit set for planning bus changes to new Link service.

Because Sound Transit did not make changes to route 545, they did not provide their travel time analysis. I suspect they analyzed trips on route 545 against the same trips on the Link 2 Line, as all trips between Redmond and Seattle on routes 545 map decently well to a single 2 Line trip. However, assuming route 545 is cut and service is added to route 542 (as proposed in 2021), a frequent route 542 with a transfer to the 1 or 2 Line at UW could also approximate any route 545 trip. Below is an analysis I did of six trips on route 545, using the same method Sound Transit used to calculate the other changes:

Trip A: Downtown Redmond to International District/Chinatown Station Trip B: Downtown Redmond to Westlake Station Trip C: Redmond Technology Station to International District/Chinatown Station Trip D: Redmond Technology Station to Westlake Station Trip E: Marymoor Village OR Bear Creek P&R to International District/Chinatown Station Trip F: Marymoor Village OR Bear Creek P&R to Westlake Station

To easily see the impact of the changes, I’ve colored cells red if times are more than 10 minutes longer, green if more than 5 minutes shorter, a shade of yellow if less than 10 minutes longer, and a shade of blue of less than 5 minutes shorter. I’ve also marked 2 Line-only travel times in italics , and 542 + 1/2 Line travel times in bold .

From the results, I think Sound Transit only analyzed the travel time impact of 2 Line-only trips, and did not consider 542 + 1/2 Line at all. Because while (to my surprise) the 2 Line competes with route 545 very well on most trips, the directness of route 545 to Redmond Technology Station makes those trips impossible to match on the 2 Line, with an added delay of 20 minutes in the worst case. But when you add in the option to take the more frequent 542 and transfer to the 1 or 2 Line at UW, this adds a faster option in the exact cases where the single 2 Line trip fares the worst against the 545. In fact, when this option is added, every case has an alternative to its route 545 trip that adds less delay than the 10 minute planning threshold Sound Transit uses, with most trips getting faster (with the most improved trip being 25 minutes faster from Marymoor to IDS).

Lastly, one thing this analysis doesn’t account for is something that you often see on route 545 toward Seattle on weekday afternoons, which are catastrophic delays. In particular, the turn from Stewart St to 5th Ave often gets so congested that route 545 buses often wait 10-20 minutes just to make this one turn. If the travel time analysis of alternative options wasn’t reason enough to move route 545 service hours elsewhere, the fact that Sound Transit is predictably wasting a large amount of service hours just waiting for this one turn just underscores how route 545 needs a second look.

If route 545 were to be deleted, this would free up a ton of service hours. Obviously the first priority would be to boost route 542 frequencies to 10 minutes peak/15 minutes midday, and extend it to Bear Creek P&R via Downtown Redmond Station (taking over the 545’s eastern section). I also think route 542 should be increased to every 15 minutes on weekends as well (something which actually wasn’t proposed in 2021 , as it kept the 542 every 30 minutes on weekends). Since half of this route 542 service already exist, this would only use up significantly less than half of route 545’s service hours.

The next priority could be restoring route 544 to South Lake Union. This was a route that Sound Transit created in March 2020 following a restructure that consolidated some service from Kirkland and Redmond to create a new route serving an emerging market for commuter service to SLU. However, being started at the beginning of the pandemic, it only operated a couple weeks before it was suspended . Originally, it proposed to be restored in 2021 as part of East Link Connections. I think this is a good idea, though I also think some changes should be made. King County Metro has shown it can run buses from SR 520 to the Mercer St exit today (something which was long though to be impossible in regular service) on route 256. Furthermore, WSDOT is planning to open a direct express lane connection between this exit and SR 520 for transit in the 2030s. So I think a restored 544 should exit at Mercer St, and could lay over at the bus layover area on Eastlake.

On the eastside, it’s also worth reevaluating whether it makes sense to run the 544 to the Overlake P&R, or even to Redmond at all. If a shorter route 544 could be made more frequent, it could facilitate 2-seat rides if moved to the right places. The way I think it could maximize connection opportunities is to serve S. Kirkland P&R, then terminate at Spring District Station, with frequencies of 8 minutes. This allows connections from routes 542 and 270 at the 520 freeway stations, some Kirkland routes at S. Kirkland, and the 2 Line at Spring District (and transfers would work well from both the east and south here).

Whether the remaining service hours after changes to the 542 go into restoring route 544 or something else entirely, what will be the case is that, while not every rider will have a faster trip, many riders will, and all riders will enjoy more frequent and consistent service across every day of the week. When express buses complement rail rather than competing with it, then both services will work better for more riders.

articles.title: Ballard Link Community Forum
articles.author: Martin Pagel
paras: Dan Strauss invited Sound Transit board members, city officials, and state officials to a Ballard Link Extension (BLE) Community Forum Monday to provide the public with information on the Ballard Link extension plans. The Nordic Museum’s auditorium was packed with residents from Ballard and along the route as well as from the Eastside and even Tacoma. After short opening remarks from the officials, Sound Transit CEO Constantine introduced Brad Owen (acting Chief Delivery Officer, former Los Angeles Metro), Lauren Matthias (who joined the BLE team as Project Director from Vancouver’s Broadway SkyTrain) and Dan Turner (long time BLE Project Manager). Then Dan Strauss took questions from the audience.

While many aspects were discussed, it became clear that Sound Transit does not envision any major changes but is focusing on reducing the cost of the project as envisioned. They are hoping Olympia will enact increasing debt allowance (by borrowing for 75 years instead of 40, which effectively reduces debt burden by $1b) and a better federal funding environment (faster grants).

Brad Owen pointed out that they already reduced the West Seattle Link Extension (WSLE) cost by $2b (after the cost had quadrupled). He said that they have already identified potential savings of $1-3b for BLE (such as a smaller trapezoidal Seattle Center station). They have just concluded an industry request for information (RFI). Some suggestions (from Alstrom, contractors, and others) had already been incorporated; others will be. In order to deliver BLE by 2042, they need to shed about $10b, otherwise it may take longer. The audience voiced concerns whether more stations would get dropped (such as Avalon and South Lake Union), and asked why WSLE was prioritized over BLE when estimates for BLE ridership are four times as high. Brad Owen pointed out that projects usually get phased in (such as L.A.’s Purple Line) and WSLE was approved first.

ST has studied automated trains. As those could not interoperate with the Rainier Line, it could only work from Ballard to Westlake and would require different trains and a separate maintenance facility. They don’t think the existing tunnel can be tapped safely to reach the existing SODO maintenance center. They would lose the regional funding (49%) currently committed for the second downtown tunnel. Brad Owen said: “In order to introduce new trains, you have to isolate the line, meaning Ballard to West Seattle, not the line extension, as it’s currently planned… Even with $2b savings for station size, we would introduce less capacity to the system and need new fleet and maintenance upgrades. It won’t actually reduce cost. We have already started to reduce the station size such as in Alaska Junction station.”

They have not studied an elevated alternative as it would require that they start the project from scratch (new scoping document). Downtown is too tight for big guideways to meet NEPA requirements (such as fire code) and would require too much utility relocations and disturbance.

While transit riders wait for BLE, somebody asked for Metro/SDOT to provide some mitigation until the line becomes available. The mayor promised to look into adding more bus lanes and discuss service improvements with Metro. Dan Strauss pointed out that express lines were cancelled during Covid and are still not reestablished. It will be important to get the Seattle Transit Measure passed and then work with Metro. KCC Baron mentioned that Metro will start a major restructure next year.
Dan Strauss reaffirmed to the audience that failure is not an option.

articles.title: Nuclear Weapons Waste Made Workers Sick. Despite a Law Meant to Help, the DOE Keeps Fighting Their Claims.
articles.author: Lizz Giordano
paras: Lonnie Rouse shuffled into a wood-paneled conference room at the Washington state Capitol in March 2018. It had been nearly a decade since medical experts diagnosed him with a neurological disease they attributed to his exposure to chemicals at work. In the time since, he had acquired a stutter, begun limping and lost several teeth biting into a banana.

For nearly 20 years, Rouse had packaged plutonium and monitored radioactive waste at the Hanford Site , a now-decommissioned Department of Energy nuclear weapons production plant in south-central Washington and one of the most contaminated nuclear sites in the country. Tanks full of radioactive sludge exposed him to at least 48 potentially hazardous chemicals . The worksite was so toxic, he said, that the floor once melted the rubber off his boots.

Rouse was among the thousands of workers responsible for the ongoing environmental cleanup at Hanford, which has been underway since the DOE shut down the last reactor in the late 1980s. Congress has acknowledged , based on voluminous studies, that radiation at DOE sites poses health risks to workers.

Over time, some people at Hanford became so sick they could no longer work. Like Rouse, they filed for workers’ compensation. The DOE consistently challenged their claims and tried to shift the blame onto the workers themselves.

By the time Rouse took his place behind then-Gov. Jay Inslee, he was desperate. His 2009 workers’ compensation claim had been denied. He had burned through his retirement savings and declared bankruptcy.
As he watched, the governor signed a bill that was supposed to change his life.

For years, Hanford employees filing workers’ compensation claims had to prove the chemicals they were exposed to on the job made them sick. The new law Inslee signed flipped that burden of proof. Under the law , agencies were instructed to presume that working at Hanford had caused certain cancers, neurological diseases and respiratory illnesses . Now the Department of Energy would have to prove to the state that something other than the job had made the workers sick if it wanted to deny their claims.

Rouse thought the presumption law would speed up his claim for benefits. State lawmakers and the former governor thought it would force the DOE to take responsibility for the harm Hanford workers were experiencing.

But despite the law, the DOE continues to fight new and existing claims, Cascade PBS and ProPublica found. We asked the state for claims records going back to the presumption law’s passage in 2018, but the state only provided records going back three and a half years, to 2023. In that period, workers filed 102 new claims for benefits, state data shows. The DOE did not recommend approving a single one.
The state, which has final say, overruled the DOE and approved 75% of those claims. The DOE appealed all but seven of those approvals.

Cascade PBS and ProPublica spoke to workers, surviving family members, lawyers representing workers and state officials. They all pointed to a pattern: The DOE systematically challenges and then drags out workers’ compensation claims for years with recommended denials and subsequent legal appeals. Along the way, it has spent millions on outside lawyers and expert testimony, including doctor evaluations that point to other causes for workers’ illnesses.

The DOE has paid out benefits to Hanford workers in some cases, lawyers and families said, but it has done so while still actively appealing the claims. It warns workers that they may have to pay the money back.

Our reporting found that not even death ends the cycle of appeals. About 152 workers’ claims remain stranded in this legal limbo — approved by the state but still under appeal by the DOE. Half of those workers are dead. The DOE continues to fight to deny their families survivors’ benefits.

“It seems pretty coldhearted, calculated, that they’re trying to save money on the back of sick workers who they made sick,” said Gerry Pollet, one of the Washington state representatives who sponsored the 2018 presumption law, who is also a co-founder of the Hanford cleanup watchdog group Heart of America Northwest. “That’s why we needed a state law.”

After Cascade PBS and ProPublica raised questions about the DOE’s pattern of litigating claims, regulators at the Washington State Department of Labor and Industries met twice with DOE staff, state agency spokesperson Carrie McCausland said. But she could not point to any other actions the agency has taken beyond the two meetings.
“Agency staff are concerned and are right now assessing the severity of patterns we’ve seen,” McCausland wrote in an email.

The DOE did not answer detailed questions or respond to the newsrooms’ findings. In a statement, a spokesperson wrote that the DOE is following “all applicable local, state, and federal laws” and “has a long and successful record of accomplishment of protecting human health and the environment.”

The DOE has the right to file multiple appeals against a claim. According to court records, its appeals have sought to overturn claims approved by the state, narrow the period of back wages, or block survivors’ benefits, among other things. In appeals filings, the DOE’s lawyers have argued that factors other than work at Hanford played a role in the workers’ illnesses, including smoking, drinking, obesity or genetics.

In Rouse’s case, the energy department blamed alcoholism and family conflicts. The state agency that handles appeals did not find those arguments persuasive. DOE awarded Rouse most of his back pay in 2024, his lawyer said. Rouse declined to say how much that was, but said he is not touching the money until the legal process concludes.
In the nearly eight years it has been fighting his claim, the DOE has filed more than 20 appeals contesting different aspects of his claim.

“We were always told that nothing is out here that’s going to harm you — you do what you are supposed to do, and you do what you are trained to do, and you’re going to be fine,” said Rouse, who now receives 24-hour care.

The smell of ammonia serves as a warning, workers say, that the underground tanks holding a mix of radioactive sludge have burped chemical vapors into the air above. From 1998 to 2008, it was Rouse’s job to monitor the toxic waste held in the “tank farms.” The containers together hold more than 50 million gallons of liquid waste. Rouse says he lost count of how many times tanks released toxic vapor that took his breath away, sometimes knocking him to the ground and making him vomit and bleed from his nose. According to a 2014 report funded by the federal government, tank farm workers exposed to chemical vapors commonly reported nausea, headaches and nosebleeds.

The liquid sloshing around in those tanks represented the radioactive byproducts of the Cold War. Hanford produced two-thirds of the plutonium for the nation’s nuclear arsenal and fueled the atomic bomb dropped on Nagasaki, Japan, in 1945.

The end of production in the late 1980s launched a cleanup effort that is expected to continue until at least 2086. As of January 2025, more than 13,000 people were working at Hanford, nearly all of them for private companies contracted by the DOE. It is one of the largest and most expensive efforts to remediate toxic waste in the nation’s history.

In 2000, Congress passed the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program Act , which provides medical care and one-time payouts to workers at DOE sites across the country. It was an acknowledgement that the nation’s nuclear weapons workers had been exposed to radioactive substances known to cause cancer. In it, lawmakers referred to a DOE policy “to litigate occupational illness claims, which has deterred workers from filing workers’ compensation claims and has imposed major financial burdens for such employees who have sought compensation.”
But the benefits of the federal program were limited: It capped payouts at $400,000.

Washington’s workers’ compensation system, by contrast, can provide steady wage replacement or a pension benefit, in some cases, for the rest of an injured employee’s life. It’s a program that can easily surpass the maximum federal benefit.

The state went further with its 2018 presumption law. Such laws generally protect firefighters who are regularly exposed to smoke, burned plastics and extreme heat. The National Council on Compensation Insurance, the Washington state attorney general and Pollet all said they were unaware of any other state that has extended that protection for radiological workers.
The federal government challenged Washington’s state law later that year in court, arguing it was discriminatory because it only applied to Hanford and the DOE.

Anticipating a Supreme Court decision that ultimately agreed, lawmakers passed an expanded version that covered all workers at “radiological hazardous waste facilities” in the state, including the state’s only functioning nuclear power plant and a French-owned facility that manufactures nuclear fuel rods. Nonetheless, roughly 75% of the 428 claims filed since 2018 have come from the DOE’s Hanford workers, according to the state Department of Labor and Industries.

Kathleen Kersey spent 10 years at Hanford, during both the production and cleanup stages. Much of her work involved measuring radiation around the site and making sure levels were safe. She says her safety training covered radiation, but not other hazards like chemical vapors burping from the waste tanks.

Kersey struggles to walk, has short-term memory problems and at one point lost vision in her right eye for three months. A doctor diagnosed her with multiple sclerosis, which is a neurological disorder, one of the categories of illnesses the state’s presumption law recognizes as related to chemical exposure at Hanford. In 2019 she filed a claim, which the state approved.
The DOE has appealed, arguing that something other than her time at Hanford caused her multiple sclerosis.
Kersey is one of the 152 workers still awaiting a resolution on her workers’ compensation claim. The DOE has not paid her any back wages, she said. The DOE declined to comment on her case.
“I feel depleted and disgusted,” Kersey said of the appeals process. “It makes me feel like I’m worthless. I have no value.”

State records show that the DOE has filed more than 500 appeals since the presumption law passed in 2018. In 20 cases, as it did with Rouse, the DOE has appealed a single worker’s claim half a dozen times or more.
“We have seen tremendous pushback from DOE on essentially almost every single case that’s been brought,” said Washington State Attorney General Nick Brown.

Rouse’s wife, Melinda, said she knew something was wrong when he could not remember how to cut an orange. His vision started to blur, he stumbled often, and suddenly he felt irritable all the time. His primary care physician first thought he might have had a brain tumor. The physician referred him to a neurologist who noted cognitive impairment, possibly due to exposure to multiple toxins at the Hanford Site. The neurologist then referred him to a neuropsychologist, who diagnosed him with “toxic encephalopathy” in 2009, saying it was “more likely than not” that chemical exposure damaged his brain, according to court records.

The U.S. Department of Labor agreed too, approving him in 2010 for benefits under the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program Act, saying it was “at least as likely as not” that Hanford contributed to his illness. A federal medical consultant even praised the neuropsychologist who assessed Rouse for his “unusually thorough analysis of causation.”
Rouse refiled his 2009 state workers’ compensation claim under the new law in 2018. Washington state approved it later that year.

articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.
